Αλλά η ηρεμία που προκύπτει από το να έχετε περισσότερα χρήματα στην τσέπη σας μπορεί να δημιουργήσει άλλα απρόβλεπτα ζητήματα. Νέα έρευνα δείχνει ότι το να γίνει κανείς πλουσιότερος μπορεί να έχει ένα κρυφό προσωπικό κόστος. Έρευνα που δημοσιεύτηκε στο Psychological Bu…
items.descriptionOriginal: Who wouldn’t want a bigger paycheck? Everyone has bills, and greater financial security certainly makes them easier to pay. But the peace of mind that comes from having more money in your pocket can generate other unforeseen issues. New research shows that getting richer might come with a hidden personal cost. Research published in Psychological Bulletin explored how paychecks and personalities shape each other. The results are a mixed bag. Making more money pays off in some ways and leaves a deficit in others. So what is it about money that “changes everything”? The study behind the surprise Researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong pooled data from 11 long-running studies covering more than 130,000 working adults around the world. Some participants were tracked for as long as 20 years. The team asked a simple question: “Do money and time change who you are?” The good news: More money, more ability to handle more problems Let’s start with the bright side. According to the study, as people earn more, they develop thicker skin. Higher earners tend to become more emotionally resilient. The buffer of a bigger paycheck helps them handle life’s daily curveballs. Stress appears not to rattle them quite as easily. At the same time, an increase in income appears to make people more reliable. Meeting deadlines and keeping commitments gets easier. A solid financial cushion reduces a lot of baseline anxiety. With their cash-flow needs met, people show up more consistently for tasks and responsibilities. Success brings useful tools for personal growth. But every coin has two sides. An uptick in salary can also affect character in less desirable ways. The hidden catch: Success is sweet, but it can sour you If more income can lead to a personality that is (1) more resilient and (2) more reliable, what’s the bad news? The first negative impact is that more wealth tends to close people off socially. The more zeros people add to their bank accounts, the less extroverted they become. The hustle for success can make people focus inward and turn away from colleagues as well as established friends and family. The second personality downside of more money is less empathy. Understanding and appreciating other people’s circumstances starts to take a back seat to fiscal ambition. Wealthy individuals often live, work, and travel in environments that insulate them from everyday struggles. When they no longer experience the reality they may have at a lower salary, they become less empathetic. How to keep the undesirable traits in check We used to think adult personalities were locked in stone. This study shows that more money can shake up that assumption. Increased income can bend a person’s personality in both positive and negative ways. It’s up to you to try to keep the less desirable traits in check as you climb the career ladder. The post Want a big raise? Experts say your personality will change in 2 great and 2 not-so-great ways. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Therapist shares 4 easy ways to stop intrusive thoughts and overthinking before they get the best of you
items.description: Τα άτομα με άγχος γνωρίζουν το γνωστό συναίσθημα του να είσαι κολλημένος στο κεφάλι σου με ανησυχία και υπερβολική σκέψη. Αυτές οι κρίσεις άγχους συχνά συνοδεύονται από ενοχλητικές σκέψεις, μηρυκασμό και υπερανάλυση. Μπορούν να σας κρατήσουν παγιδευμένους. Σύμφωνα με την Emma McAdam, LMFT, αδειούχο θεραπεύτρια γάμου και οικογένειας και ιδρύτρια του Therapy in a Nutshell, ο τρόπος…
items.descriptionOriginal: People with anxiety know the familiar feeling of being stuck in your head with worry and overthinking . These bouts of anxiety often come with intrusive thoughts, rumination , and overanalyzing. They can keep you feeling trapped. According to Emma McAdam, LMFT, a licensed marriage and family therapist and founder of Therapy in a Nutshell , the way to fix these thoughts is to retrain your brain. “Your brain secretly believes that overthinking is protecting you,” McAdam said. The 4 types of overthinking McAdam explained that there are four different types of overthinking: worry, intrusive thoughts, overplanning or overanalyzing, and rumination. She broke each one down. Type #1: Worry McAdam shared that worry is the “fuel” of anxiety disorders. “Worry is where you’re constantly thinking about what could go wrong in the future,” she explained, noting that it contributes to chronic stress fueled by the stress hormones cortisol and adrenaline. Type #2: Intrusive thoughts McAdam cited a study that found that 94% of people report having intrusive thoughts—so if you have them, you are not alone. Examples of intrusive thoughts include: What if I hurt someone else? What if I do something sexually inappropriate? What if I swerve into traffic? What if I don’t really love my partner? What if I touch some bad germs? What if I lose control? View this post on Instagram Type #3: Overplanning or overanalyzing This type of overthinking is the nervous system’s attempt to manage anxiety by controlling outcomes. When the brain is overplanning, as McAdam explained, it can run scenarios in your mind, make lists, rewrite messages, or try to avoid mistakes. These messages can look like: If I say it just right, no one will be upset. If I plan this trip perfectly, nothing will go wrong. If I analyze enough, I won’t get hurt. Type #4: Rumination McAdam defined rumination as “literally chewing on the past.” It is “where you keep dwelling on your past mistakes, or the wrongs you were wronged. Where you wish you’d done something differently, or taken a different path, or just had the eagles drop you off at Mordor.” Rumination is also the fuel for “depression, hopelessness, and despair.” 4 easy ways to stop overthinking Each type of overthinking has a different solution. Here’s how to stop each one, according to McAdam: #1: How to stop worrying McAdam explained that when worry arises, the brain does something called “brain math.” Brain math sends this signal: “‘Phew, all that worrying kept my human alive. I’ve gotta do that again, so that she doesn’t die again,’” said McAdam. “And the cycle of worry just triggers over and over again.” To stop this, she suggested making a habit of “scheduled worry.” “You tell your brain when to worry. Every day at a regular time, like 5 p.m., you’re going to sit down for 20 minutes and worry on paper (write it down),” she said. Doing this trains your brain that it’s OK to worry—just at specific times of the day. To get into a groove with it, McAdam recommended setting an alarm each day at a set time. #2: How to stop intrusive thoughts The best way to handle intrusive thoughts is to think of them like an explosive device that needs to be defused. McAdam explained that this is called cognitive defusion. When an intrusive thought comes to your mind, you tell your brain: “‘Thank you for that thought. Thanks for trying to keep me safe. I’m good.’ You notice it? Name it: ‘That’s an intrusive thought,’” she said. If it doesn’t go away, the next step is to respond by redirecting your attention to be present in the moment by saying, “Maybe, maybe not.” Redirect your attention back to the present moment. “There are a few other ways to practice cognitive defusion. Sing the thought in a ridiculous voice, over and over,” she added. “Imagine the thought as a ‘part’,” said McAdam. “Give it a name. ‘Oh there’s Negative Nancy again,’ or ‘there’s Bob; he’s always worried,’” she recommended. View this post on Instagram #3: How to stop overanalyzing and overplanning McAdam said that for the brain to stop overplanning or overanalyzing, it must shift its focus from control to trust. “Trust in yourself that you can handle it. You can’t just tell your brain to do this; you have to show your brain that you can handle uncertainty by doing something imperfectly,” she said. For example, she suggested taking a spontaneous trip without “having every detail figured out,” or “say something silly in a social setting and watch how people don’t actually care.” These things will retrain your brain to have less anxiety and help you no longer feel the need to overanalyze or overplan. #4: How to stop rumination To stop ruminating, McAdam said the goal is to “identify the value, and then take action on it here in the present.” One example she offered is when rumination comes with regret about a past mistake, break it into two parts: the value and the present-moment action. Value: “So what do you really value? A value is something within your control. I value trying hard. I value learning from my mistakes. I value taking responsibility. And the best thing about values is that you can always take action in the present,” McAdam explained. Present-moment action: Fix one small part Apologize Learn one thing “By acting on your values, you shift out of rumination toward action here in the present moment,” said McAdam. The post Therapist shares 4 easy ways to stop intrusive thoughts and overthinking before they get the best of you appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: It takes many people to run a large cruise liner, with mega-ships employing up to 2,300 people at a time. On average, a cruise ship hires one staff member for every 2.25 passengers. But on some luxury liners , the ratio drops to 1:1. The sheer number of people it takes to run a ship raises a big question: how much do they get paid? Royal Caribbean dancer Alley Kerr, known on social media as Wanderlust Alley , got personal about how much she makes as a cruise ship performer. Her pay varies depending on whether she’s on land or at sea and which responsibilities she takes on as a performer. For those of us who work on land, that money means something totally different because life at sea comes with an incredible number of perks. When you work on a cruise ship, the biggest benefit is that you don’t have to pay rent, though your living space in the crew cabin is small. You also get free meals on board, though some fine dining may be off-limits or available for a small fee. You also receive full health benefits. Another incredible perk is free access to ports, and depending on the schedule, you may be able to visit some wonderful destinations when the ship docks. How much does a cruise ship performer get paid on land? In her video, Kerr admitted she doesn’t make much money when the ship is docked in a port between destinations or when her team is preparing for new performances. “Staff are probably getting paid more now, but I got paid $300 a week. So that ends up being about $1,328 per month which, even though you’re not paying rent, it’s honestly not a lot,” Kerr said. Even though when she’s “on land” she has a place to stay in a cruise cabin, the normal perks, including all-inclusive food, aren’t available. “I find that during this time, for a lot of dancers especially, it’s a net loss. Sure, there are ways to budget and everything, but grocery stores are not close by, everything is really far away, and then even though you’re getting housed, it has nothing in it, so you end up spending quite a bit on services like food, Ubers, and cleaning supplies.” How much does a cruise ship performer get paid at sea? Things get much better for Kerr when Royal Caribbean sets sail, where she receives $ 3,800 a month as a base rate. “As a dancer/vocalist in a Broadway show, they’re paying for me to know the shows, maintain the shows, rehearse the shows, and then as well as do things like Muster 2.0 [Royal Caribbean safety drills], spotting and dressing for the ice skaters, and then pretty much any other thing that the cruise director would ask us to do in the realm of entertainment,” she continues. Cruise ships at a dock. Photo credit: Canva But base pay is just the beginning of her salary; there are several ways she can add to her salary: Fly pay: Being an aerial performer is an additional $450 a month . Singing: Performing as a vocalist is an extra $1,000 a month . Understudy pay: Being prepared to step in when the regular performer can’t make it on stage is another $180 a month. She gets an additional $100 per performance when she steps in and takes over the role. Company manager/Dance captain: When she takes on additional managerial roles, she receives an additional $1200 a month. All in all, on this cruise contract from two years ago, Kerr made about $6500 a month at sea. If Kerr spent the entire year at sea, she’d make around $78,000, above the national average of $70,000 . She also gets free food and rent, which saves her at least $25,000 a year. So, if you can handle life at sea, away from friends and family, working as a cruise ship performer isn’t a bad way to make a living. The post A cruise ship performer broke down her monthly paycheck, and it’s all about the perks appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένα «απλό» μαθηματικό πρόβλημα έχει χωρίσει τους ανθρώπους 50/50. Είναι μια μεγάλη μεταφορά για τον κοινωνικό διαχωρισμό.
items.titleOriginal: A ‘simple’ math problem has divided people 50/50. It’s a great metaphor for social division.
items.description: Θεωρητικά, ένα μαθηματικό πρόβλημα που περιλαμβάνει τέσσερα μονοψήφια και βασική αριθμητική —χωρίς αλγεβρικές συναρτήσεις, χωρίς μεταβλητές, χωρίς εκθέτες— θα πρέπει να είναι εύκολο για κάθε απόφοιτο λυκείου να λύσει. items.descriptionOriginal: In theory, a math problem involving four single digits and basic arithmetic—no algebraic functions, no variables, no exponents—should be easy for any high school graduate to solve. So why are people split right down the middle on the answer to this seemingly simple problem ? 6 ÷ 2 (1+2) = ? You may have gotten 9. You may have gotten 1. If you take this poll shared by World of Statistics on X, you’ll see how others answered. As of this article’s writing, over 1.3 million people have voted, and the split is nearly 50/50. 6 ÷ 2 (1 + 2) = — World of Statistics (@stats_feed) October 26, 2026 Why this problem presents as a perfect metaphor for social division We’ll get into the actual math problem and why people are so split on the solution shortly. But to me, the debates surrounding it represent something bigger. Nearly every element of the problem, its solutions, and people’s insistence that their answer is correct is a metaphor for divisions in society. It really is that deep. Stick with me here. Many of us think math has strict rules and definitions because we were taught that early on. We likely learned that multiple methods can solve an equation, but they should ultimately lead to the same answer. Basic math is straightforward. Answers are either right or wrong, and if you get the wrong answer, you messed up your calculations somewhere. We’ve internalized that idea as fact since childhood. But what if some problems just aren’t that simple? The vehemence with which people insist they are right One way the divided responses to this math equation reflect social divisions is in people’s insistence that their solution is correct. Some folks are adamant that the answer is 9, and anyone who says otherwise is “a moron” and the reason “we are doomed.” We also have people insisting the answer is 1, and anyone who says differently “doesn’t fully understand math” and “needs to go back to school.” 1+2 =3 2(3) =6 6/6 =1 gotta do the things in the parenthesis first then 2(3) are together so technically u do that next n then u divide — gmo nikita (@nikitalyse) October 26, 2026 The vehemence with which people argue that their answer is correct and disparage those who came to a different conclusion is familiar, isn’t it? Instead of saying, “Huh, I came up with a different answer. What are we seeing differently in the problem that led us to different solutions?” we have people saying, “I’m right. You’re wrong and also an idiot.” Hold that thought while we do the math. The role our education plays in understanding problems and solutions The biggest source of disagreement with this problem appears to stem from what people learned about math in school. The order-of-operations rule (memorized through acronyms like PEMDAS or BOMDAS) plays a big role. Here’s the problem again: 6 ÷ 2 (1+2) = ? Those with a solid grasp of PEMDAS felt secure in their answer of 9. Following the order of operations, you must calculate inside the parentheses first, then multiply and divide from left to right, which makes the equation 6 ÷ 2 • 3 = 9. Those who have studied math in different contexts, such as physics, or who have learned different conventions are likely to see 2 (1+2) as implied (or implicit) multiplication, also known as juxtaposition. The lack of an actual multiplication symbol (x or •) as part of the equation means 2 (1+2) is essentially treated as a singular term. So we end up multiplying 2(3) first, which gives us 6 ÷ 6 = 1. (Don’t argue with me. Argue with the mathematician who explains the PEMDAS paradox. ) The problem is actually the problem itself So which answer is right? Technically, both. Isn’t that maddening? (But maybe a little freeing, if we can accept it?) Mathematicians have explained that this math problem is ambiguous the way it is written, which is why people solve it differently and get different answers. Mathematically, there isn’t enough context to interpret the problem and solve it in a “correct” way. It’s either a “gotcha” problem designed to create the debate we’re seeing or a poorly written problem that should be notated differently. That also feels familiar, doesn’t it? How often do we see people talk about societal problems and solutions while leaving out necessary context? A lot. And what we end up with is people arguing over solutions with no way to agree because the problem itself is poorly presented. (Or purposefully presented with missing context to create division—politicians pay consultants big money to determine how problems should be framed to justify their preferred solutions.) Away from black-and-white thinking, and toward more clearly defined problems One of the biggest problems with modern social discourse is simplistic, black-and-white thinking. The further you advance in math, however, the less black-and-white it becomes, and the same should go for our thinking as we deepen our understanding of social issues. We also have a clarity problem. In the YouTube video above, Dr. Trefor Bazett, an associate teaching professor of mathematics at the University of Victoria in Canada, shares in his explanation of this math problem debate: “The whole point of using symbols in mathematics is so that I can communicate with you—that a complex, complicated idea, I can convey it in a clear and unambiguous way. And if I’m not doing that, if I’ve written something down that leads to a viral math problem controversy trending, then what that means is that I am using a bad choice of symbols.” Politicians and other powerful people love presenting problems ambiguously. They hire consultants to frame problems vaguely enough to keep them out of trouble but specifically enough to lead people toward their preferred solutions. We need to insist on clearly defining the problems we face, or we’ll keep digging into solutions that are equally right within our own understandings. Being right doesn’t always mean others are wrong We won’t always see eye to eye on everything. Some real-world social issues are inherently ambiguous, so perfect clarity isn’t always possible. But perhaps if we could resist the urge to say, “I’m right. You’re wrong and also an idiot,” when discussing problems, we could actually solve a lot more of them. Imagine if we took a beat when we disagree and said, “What are we seeing differently in the problem that led us to different solutions?” And what if we went even further to, “Yeah, I can see how you got there. Here’s how and why I got to my answer.” That approach may not make for good social media drama, but it sure seems like it could help us get a little closer to agreement on solutions to real-world problems. The post A ‘simple’ math problem has divided people 50/50. It’s a great metaphor for social division. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Spider silk can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking. They are investigating ways to produce spider silk artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal. The key challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber. Strength like steel Spider silk is a biomaterial produced by these arachnids, and it is mostly in the form of threadlike fiber with high elasticity and strength comparable to steel. The interesting thing about this silk is that it comes in many forms, each with its own purpose. While thin threads are the most familiar form, which the spiders use to make webs, there are a few other forms as well that this animal uses – sometimes to catch a prey or to protect eggs, or to use it as a safety rope. Among its many properties, spider silk’s tensile strength is quite intriguing, reaching up to 1.5 billion pascals (GPa). That means it can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking. This is comparable to high-grade steel. Due to their tensile strength, toughness, light weight, and biodegradability , they have a potential for their usage, especially in the textile industry. Researchers are investigating ways to produce it artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal, and they can’t be raised in large numbers like silkworms because they are cannibalistic. Scaling up is challenging University of North Carolina (UNC) ‘s Sarah Stellwagen, who studies silk from arthropods (insects and arachnids) at the material and genetic levels, said in an interview that the challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber. “Researchers have made plenty of protein soup, as a spider does, but unlike spiders, they haven’t been able to spin that protein into solid threads at a scale that is relevant for the public,” said Stellwagen, who is an assistant professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at UNC Charlotte. The spider does this by passing the fluid from its gland through a narrow duct, changing its chemical environment and assembling it into a tightly packed structure called a beta-sheet. The fiber then emerges through its spinnerets in the solid form. However, there has been some progress as well. Researchers at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) have shown that protein can be produced in larger quantities and more efficiently, which can also reduce production costs. Researchers Anna Rising and Benjamin Schmuck, who earlier this year received a grant of EUR 200,000 from H&M Foundation, are now working to produce fibers and yarn from protein for textile tests. The group is also exploring the fiber’s use for medical purposes. “The award (grant and support program) gives us the opportunity to take the next step: do more trials, improve the manufacturing process, and produce enough material to test yarn and textiles,” says Anna Rising, professor at the Department of Animal Biosciences. Earlier research from King’s College London and San Diego State University (SDSU) in California has decoded the “molecular stickers” that make spider silk stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists at UC San Francisco have engineered CAR-T cells that stay dormant until they reach the brain, where they switch on and destroy tumor cells. In mice, these CAR-T cells were able to clear diffuse midline glioma (DMG), a lethal form of childhood brain cancer that integrates into healthy tissue. The cells also had staying power. When scientists introduced another round of cancer several weeks later, the cells were still able to fight.

items.descriptionOriginal: Another exciting step forward for women’s health: Four major health societies teamed up to create the first shared framework and clinical guidance for women’s heart health, tailored to distinct life phases — from first menstruation to postmenopause. The much-needed update comes from the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. Because while cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in women, medical research has historically centered on men’s symptoms and physiology (which differ from women in myriad ways), thus reducing the quality of care women receive on average. This landmark move seeks to change that. The new framework organizes women’s cardiovascular care into four chronological life stages that account for hormonal and biological transitions, plus pregnancy. In addition to getting clinicians on the same page about women’s cardiovascular health, the system and its accompanying guidance can help them identify risks earlier and take necessary action before problems worsen. https://iprsoftwaremedia.com/67/files/20269/07b6ae0ca5d8a720af4942e310f02184/Dr.%20Khan%20on%20whole%20life%20view%20of%20womens%20heart%20health.mp4 “Women experience their health care across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” Dr. Sadiya S. Khan, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, said in a news release. She noted that the updates, a trio of scientific papers published this week, “connect the dots” for providers across health domains, so holistic care can begin in adolescence. Khan added that the approach emphasizes that cardiovascular health can’t be fully understood by looking only at the heart. “We need to recognize that women’s heart health is deeply interconnected with hormonal and emotional health,” she said. The Stages Stage 1: Perimenarche The first stage comprises the transition that occurs around the first menstrual period, generally taking place between ages 8 and 15. In an essay for Time , Khan wrote that a first period before age 10 can serve as a signal of higher cardiovascular risk. “Heart health begins long before adulthood,” Dr. Amanda Marma Perak, vice-chair of the collaborative writing group and a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital, added in the news release. “As pediatric clinicians, we have the opportunity to help every girl start strong and to ensure that what we learn about her health follows her as she grows.” Stage 2: Ovarian Cycling This stage represents the approximate ages of 15-44, when regular ovulation and hormone cycles are established. Pregnancy most often occurs during these years. “Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) can frequently disrupt sleep, physical activity, and eating patterns, which are relevant to cardiovascular health,” Khan wrote for Time. “These symptoms are common, but being common does not make them inconsequential.” Heavy or irregular bleeding can also act as indicators. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (formerly known as PCOS), for example, has been associated with a significant increase in risk for heart disease. Stage 3: Perimenopause Stage 3 represents the transition from regular to variable cycles, skipped periods, and hormone changes, taking place around ages 45-51. “Recognizing perimenopause as a distinct life stage acknowledges that its symptoms can disrupt daily life, persist for years, and deserve treatment,” wrote Khan. “Hormone and nonhormonal treatments can help, with decisions guided by symptoms, age, cardiovascular and cancer history, and a woman’s preferences. The same visit offers an opportunity to assess cardiovascular disease risk and address changes in cholesterol and cardiometabolic health.” Stage 4: Postmenopause Representing the years following menopause, which begins 12 months after one’s final period, this stage can account for 40% of a woman’s life. It occurs at approximately 51 years and older. The news release notes that most heart attacks, strokes, and heart-failure events occur during this stage — but are more than 80% preventable when steps are taken early. Pregnancy (in Any Life Stage) The framework identifies the time before, during, and after pregnancy “as a biological ‘stress test’ that can identify cardiovascular risks that may have been previously unrecognized,” per the release, which highlights postpartum care as a “missed opportunity” for many women. “Only about 60% of U.S. women with high blood pressure-related complications during pregnancy receive follow-up care for their high blood pressure within six months of delivery,” it states, noting that the American Heart Association is calling for immediate action to address that gap. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” Khan said. “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share.”

items.descriptionOriginal: What if you could build an office, security checkpoint, or robotics facility using Lego-like blocks? The structure could be assembled near where it is needed, expanded as requirements grow, and even dismantled and moved to another location. Two U.S. companies are working to turn that idea into reality. Florida-based Tesseract Ventures Tuesday announced an initiative to develop modular technology-enabled infrastructure in partnership with Kentucky-based Lok-N-Blok that can be rapidly deployed and customized for different applications. The infrastructure, called Tesseract Synthetic Brick Technology Kits, will use Lok-N-Blok’s modular building components, which resemble Lego-like blocks . ​Rather than adding technology to conventional buildings or shipping containers, the kits are designed with the technology built into the structure from the beginning, the company said in a statement. Tailored to needs ​According to the company, the systems can be digitally designed, packaged for transport, assembled near the deployment site, expanded as requirements change, and dismantled and redeployed elsewhere. ​To meet the customer’s needs, Tesseract will tailor the finished solutions, read the statement. Depending on the application, the kits could include sensors, cameras, communications equipment, drone storage and launch systems, robotic fabrication equipment, and other integrated technologies. ​”We see an opportunity to rethink the relationship between infrastructure and technology,” said John Boucard, Founder and CEO of Tesseract Ventures. “Instead of putting our technology inside a box that was designed for something else, Tesseract Synthetic Brick Technology Kits allow us to design the structure around the mission.” ​Company officials said the kits can start as small installations using standardized building blocks and technology modules before expanding into larger operational environments. ​”Lok-N-Blok was created around the idea that construction could become more modular, efficient, and adaptable,” said John Lewis, CEO of Lok-N-Blok. “Tesseract brings a powerful technology layer to that idea. Together, we have an opportunity to explore how modular construction can become the foundation for intelligent, rapidly deployable operational environments,” he added. Reusable components to fit different roles ​Beyond rapid deployment, the companies are positioning reusability as another key advantage. Standardized technology components can be reused to create different configurations without redesigning an entire system for every deployment. ​The partnership could also enable Tesseract to develop reusable technology packages, such as Access & Security, Smart Space, Drone Operations, Communications, Sensor, and Forge Fabrication kits, that can be incorporated into different structural configurations. ​Initially, the companies expect the technology kits to serve four key markets: defense, construction, critical infrastructure, and agriculture, the statement read . ​In defense, the systems could support drone operations, forward command centers, communications nodes, sensor hubs, and mobile fabrication capabilities. Construction applications include project command centers, secure workspaces, guard stations, and autonomous drone inspection stations. ​For critical infrastructure, the kits could be used as remote operations centers, emergency-response facilities, utility inspection hubs, and communications nodes. In agriculture, the systems are envisioned as field operations centers, drone stations, equipment hubs, and distributed farm intelligence facilities. ​

items.descriptionOriginal: This Sunday, the clocks will “fall back”—as the battle over daylight saving time continues. In July, the House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. But research shows that daylight saving time doesn’t actually save energy or increase productivity. Instead, sleep researchers like Susan Kohl Malone , assistant professor at New York University Rory Meyers College of Nursing, agree that daylight standard time is more aligned with our biology. The later sunrise of daylight saving time “leads to permanent disruption of our natural biological rhythms. We need morning sunlight to get us up and going,” explains Malone. Malone notes that switching the clock in the spring comes with its own issues, including an increase in car accidents and heart attacks in the week that follows. “Changing clock times is not good for us, but the bill now in the Senate would lock Americans out of sync with the sun,” she writes in the Boston Globe . “A brighter winter evening is a poor trade for a darker, groggier, unhealthier winter morning.” Source: New York University The post Why permanent daylight saving time is a bad idea for health appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: New research explores how perceptions of immunity can shape vaccine decisions and how personalized feedback may help people better understand their protection. When it’s time for another vaccine, many people may ask themselves a familiar question: Do I really need another one? The answer may depend, at least in part, on how protected they think they already are. Allie Sinclair, an assistant professor of psychological sciences and director of Rice University’s Learning & Behavior Change Lab, and her collaborators at Duke University found that people often misjudged their level of immunity to COVID-19. Many believed they were more protected than their vaccination and infection histories suggested, while others underestimated their protection and may have been more concerned about their risk than necessary. Those perceptions matter because what people believe about their immunity can influence whether they get vaccinated, take a diagnostic test when symptoms appear, or take other steps to protect their health. The study in PNAS Nexus sought to better understand why people were not staying up to date on recommended COVID-19 vaccines. The researchers’ earlier work pointed to a potential blind spot: People may know another vaccine is available but believe they are already sufficiently protected. If someone feels overconfident in their protection, they might believe that a vaccine dose doesn’t offer much benefit. “We expected that factors like inconvenience and concern about side effects would be important, but to our surprise, we found that some of the most common reasons were related to overconfidence in immunity,” Sinclair says. “People believed that they were still protected and so didn’t stand to benefit from a vaccine dose.” That led the researchers to develop an interactive “ Immunity Estimator ” tool that gives users personalized feedback about their likely protection against COVID-19. Users enter the approximate month and year of previous COVID-19 vaccinations and infections. The tool then estimates their likely protection against infection and severe disease based on factors including the number and timing of those events, changes in the virus, and the rate at which antibodies decline. Researchers tested the approach with 882 US adults, ages 18 to 93. Participants received either personalized feedback from the Immunity Estimator, an informational flyer produced by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or a modified version of the flyer that included information about waning immunity. The researchers aimed to test whether the personalized feedback about immunity was more effective than these existing, impersonal methods of encouraging vaccination. The personalized approach was the most effective at bringing participants’ perceptions of their risk more closely in line with actual risk (estimated based on each person’s history of vaccines and infections). It worked in both directions, increasing perceived risk among people who underestimated it and decreasing perceived risk among those who overestimated it. The effect was particularly strong among older adults, who are more vulnerable to severe disease and can most benefit from maintaining protection. Sinclair says the Immunity Estimator was designed to tap into two processes involved in how people learn and make decisions. “First, we used corrective feedback because surprising information, or prediction error, engages brain systems that support learning and belief updating,” she says. “Second, we gave participants personalized information because self-relevance is a key part of the brain’s value calculation system, used to guide choices.” Simply put, general information about vaccines or waning immunity may not resonate in the same way as information that shows someone what it could mean for them personally. And the effect lasted. When researchers followed up two months later, participants’ perceptions of risk remained more closely aligned with the researchers’ estimates. Among those who were eligible for an updated vaccine but had not received one when the study began, participants who received information about waning immunity also reported higher vaccine uptake than the national increase during the same period. The researchers caution that the study was not large enough to establish significant differences in vaccine uptake among the three intervention groups. Still, the results suggest that addressing what people believe about their existing immunity could be an important part of vaccine communication. “Prior studies have shown that interventions that focus on just providing information or increasing knowledge tend to have very weak downstream effects on beliefs, intentions and behaviors,” Sinclair says. “Giving people personalized information that targets specific beliefs related to a behavior can be more effective.” Although the research focused on COVID-19, Sinclair sees broader potential for the approach. It could be adapted for recurring vaccines such as the annual flu shot, though researchers would need to develop disease-specific ways of estimating immunity. The implications could extend beyond vaccines. Misjudging personal risk can shape other health decisions, from whether someone takes a diagnostic test when symptoms appear to choices about preventive care and healthy behaviors. “Our beliefs about personal risk and protection are foundational for many preventative health behaviors, like getting an annual checkup or living a healthy lifestyle,” Sinclair says. “Providing personalized feedback could help people make more informed decisions in many areas of life to help them stay healthy.” Source: Rice University The post Perceptions of immunity shape vaccine decisions appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Few things bring as much joy to a parent’s heart as the adorable sounds their babies make. But back in 2020, when a dad with a vision, a camera and a year’s worth of footage used those sounds to recreate one of the most iconic rock songs ever…let’s just say joy alone doesn’t quite cover it. In one of the most epically adorable and adorably epic song renditions ever, dad and video editor Matt MacMillan spliced together tiny snippets of his baby’s sounds to make AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck.” And it’s one of those things you just have to see to believe. A rock anthem, baby edition Below, enjoy little Ryan singing a jaw-droppingly awesome babyfied version of “Thunderstruck.” Nothing but awe and respect for a guy who takes a whole year to get just the right sounds at the right pitches and figures out how to put them together to create this masterpiece: Making a sneeze into a cymbal? Are you kidding me? People have been understandably impressed, with the video getting over 11 million views. “Ryan becomes the vocalist of AB/CD.” “I need a cover in 17 years whenever he is an adult singing over the instrumentals lol” “‘I recorded my son for a full year. I edited for the next 5.'” “The fact that he genuinely found clips that fit every note he need instead of just pitch shifting like most videos like this do really makes this stand out. Good job he’s adorable.” “This dude had a kid just so he could make this song. What a Legend.” “Other parents: ‘I want my child to create masterpieces.’ This guy: ‘my child IS the masterpiece.'” “I’m a residential plumber and I’ve had an absolutely horrible day on a work shift that’s lasted 13 hours and even after crawling through human poop all day this made me smile laugh and giggle like a small baby.” How the dad pulled it off Believe it or not, it’s not autotuned or pitch-shifted. Those notes are all baby. The real question is: How did he do it? This isn’t just some autotune trick. According to MacMillan’s explainer video, he did it all manually, going through each video clip of Baby Ryan, organizing the 83 usable ones by pitch and figuring out what notes they were. Perhaps most impressively, he didn’t even know the notes of “Thunderstruck” to begin with and doesn’t really read music. He had to pluck the song out on the piano and then match those notes with his baby’s sounds. As he wrote, “It took forever.” But he shared an inside look at how he did it here: Seriously, doesn’t seeing how he did it make it even more impressive? Pure human creativity and perseverance on display. What a delightful gift Ryan will have for the rest of his life. Much better than a standard baby book. This wasn’t his first baby cover Baby Ryan’s “Thunderstruck” was not MacMillan’s first foray into baby covers, either. He previously created a rendition of “Carol of the Bells” using Baby Ella’s sounds, and it is just as impressive (and adorable) as Baby Ryan’s. Here’s one to add to your holiday playlist: Here’s to the humans who wow us with their ambitious, innovative projects that exist purely to bring a smile to people’s faces. You can follow Matt MacMillan on YouTube. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Dad remakes AC/DC’s ‘Thunderstruck’ using only a year’s worth of baby’s recorded sounds appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Ο συγγραφέας George Orwell είναι περισσότερο γνωστός για τα βιβλία του 1984 και Animal Farm. Ο Όργουελ ήταν ένας παραγωγικός συγγραφέας γνωστός για τα πολιτικά μυθιστορήματα και τα δοκίμιά του. Η ζωή του τελείωσε το 1950 σε ηλικία μόλις 46 ετών μετά από μάχη με την προχωρημένη φυματίωση…
items.descriptionOriginal: Author George Orwell is best known for his books 1984 and Animal Farm . He was an English novelist whose real name was Eric Arthur Blair, according to the Orwell Foundation . Orwell was a prolific writer known for his politically themed novels and essays. His life came to an end in 1950 at just 46 years old after a battle with advanced tuberculosis. But in those short years, his writing came to inspire millions of readers around the world. In 1946, Orwell shared a few of his writing rules with readers in an essay titled “Politics and the English Language.” The essay features Orwell’s commentary on the craft of writing, according to Douglas E. Abrams , a University of Missouri law professor. In his paper “ Orwell’s Six Cures to Bad Writing ,” Abrams writes that for Orwell, “Good writing depends on sound grammar, spelling, style, and syntax, but it also depends on willingness to bend or break the ‘rules’ when advisable.” View this post on Instagram Orwell didn’t hold back his opinion Orwell warned that the English language is “in a bad way,” and Abrams summarizes his diagnosis this way: “debased” prose was marked by “abuse,” “slovenliness,” and a “lifeless, imitative style” nearly devoid of “a fresh, vivid, home-made turn of speech,” while a “tendency … away from concreteness” had left writing “dreary,” “ugly and inaccurate.” Orwell’s verdict: “This mixture of vagueness and sheer incompetence is the most marked characteristic of modern English prose, and especially of any kind of political writing.” Specifically, Orwell shared six rules he stood by to help others write clearly and concisely. Orwell wrote that choosing your words and then deciding what impression they’ll make on the reader “cuts out all stale or mixed images, all prefabricated phrases, needless repetitions, and humbug and vagueness generally.” “But one can often be in doubt about the effect of a word or a phrase, and one needs rules that one can rely on when instinct fails,” he wrote. “I think the following rules will cover most cases.” George Orwell’s Six Rules for Writing Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print. Never use a long word where a short one will do. If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out. Never use the passive where you can use the active. Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent. Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. 80 years later, it still holds up Although Orwell’s advice dates back to 1946, writers today still credit his tips with making them better writers. People on Reddit shared how his rules have impacted their ability to write. “George Orwell’s writing advice is amazingly instructive when it comes to writing with clarity,” one person wrote. Another commented, “Following the first two rules changed my writing completely (for the better), I think sometime in college. I think people mistake those rules to mean ‘ always use a shorter word or fewer words,’ which isn’t the case. But it takes some experience to figure out good exceptions to the rules.” Another writer noted, “I think it’s literally follow 1-5, unless it reads better to break them, then use 6. If you aren’t writing for yourself, write something your readers will understand without a dictionary or reference texts. Knowing your audience is extremely important; I feel these rules are especially important when writing about fields with their own ‘language’ (words used in ways the common person would not assume).” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post George Orwell shared ‘6 rules for writing’ in 1946. People say they’re more essential than ever. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Any time discussions of wealth and poverty come up, people inevitably start talking about boots. The standard phrase that usually gets thrown around is “pull yourself up by your bootstraps ,” which is shorthand for “work harder and don’t ask for or expect help.” (The fact that the phrase was originally used sarcastically because pulling oneself up by one’s bootstraps is physically impossible is rarely acknowledged, but c’est la vie.) The idea that people who build wealth are able to do so because they individually work harder than poor people is baked into the American consciousness and wrapped up in the ideal of the American dream. A different take on boots and building wealth, however, paints a more accurate picture of what it takes to get out of poverty. A good pair of work boots will save you money in the long run, but only if you can afford them in the first place. Photo credit: Canva A fantasy author’s take on boots Author Terry Pratchett died in 2015, but his writing lives on and is occasionally shared on his official social media accounts. In January 2022, his official Twitter account (now X) shared what Pratchett called the “Captain Samuel Vimes ‘Boots’ theory of socio-economic unfairness” from Pratchett’s 1993 book Men At Arms . This boots theory explains that one reason the rich are able to get richer is because they are able to spend less money. The thread supported UK anti-poverty campaigner Jack Monroe’s proposed “Vimes Boots Index,” which Pratchett’s estate authorized to track the price of basic goods. Monroe said the UK’s Office for National Statistics then announced it would change how it reports food-price inflation across income levels, though the ONS did not say that was a response to her campaign. If that sounds confusing, read on: … He earned thirty-eight dollars a month plus allowances. A really good pair of leather boots cost fifty dollars. But an affordable pair of boots, which were sort of okay for a season or two and then leaked like hell when the cardboard gave out, cost about ten dollars… 2/5 — Terry Pratchett ? ?? ? (@terryandrob) January 25, 2022 Pratchett wrote: “The reason that the rich were so rich, Vimes reasoned, was because they managed to spend less money. Take boots, for example. He earned thirty-eight dollars a month plus allowances. A really good pair of leather boots cost fifty dollars. But an affordable pair of boots, which were sort of OK for a season or two and then leaked like hell when the cardboard gave out, cost about ten dollars. Those were the kind of boots Vimes always bought, and wore until the soles were so thin that he could tell where he was in Ankh-Morpork on a foggy night by the feel of the cobbles. But the thing was that good boots lasted for years and years. A man who could afford fifty dollars had a pair of boots that’d still be keeping his feet dry in ten years’ time, while the poor man who could only afford cheap boots would have spent a hundred dollars on boots in the same time and would still have wet feet.” This was the Captain Samuel Vimes ‘Boots’ theory of socio-economic unfairness. Why cheap boots cost more In other words, people who have the money to spend a little more upfront often end up spending less in the long run. A $50 pair of boots that last five years essentially cost you $10 a year. But if you can only afford $10 upfront for a pair of boots that last six months, that’s what you buy, and you end up paying twice as much over a five-year period. There are so many areas in which this principle applies when you’re poor. Buying in bulk saves you money over the long run, but you have to be able to afford the bulk cost up front. A reliable car that doesn’t require regular repairs will cost more than a beater, but if the beater is all you can afford, that’s what you’re stuck with. You’ll likely spend the same or more over time than if you’d bought a newer/higher quality car, but without the capital (or the credit rating) to begin with, you don’t have much choice. People who can afford larger down payments pay lower interest rates, saving them money both immediately and in the long run. People who can afford to buy more can spend more with credit cards, pay off the balances, build up good credit and qualify for lower interest rate loans. There are lots of good financial decisions and strategies one can utilize if one has the ability to build up some cash. But if you are living paycheck to paycheck, you can’t. The bottom rung is out of reach Climbing the financial ladder requires getting to the bottom rung first. Those who started off anywhere on the ladder can make all kinds of pronouncements about how to climb it: good, sound advice that really does work if you’re already on the ladder. But for people living in poverty, the bottom rung is just out of reach, and the walls you have to climb to get to it are slippery. It’s expensive to be poor. It’s hard to climb out of poverty when you can’t reach the ladder. Photo credit: Canva When people talk about how hard it is to climb out of poverty , this is a big part of what they mean. Ladder-climbing advice is useless if you can’t actually get to the ladder. And yet, far too many people decry offering people assistance that might help them reach the ladder so they can start taking advantage of all that great financial advice. Why? Perhaps because they were born somewhere on the ladder, even if it was the bottom rung, and aren’t aware that there are people for whom the ladder is out of reach. Or perhaps they’re unaware of how expensive it is to be poor and how the costs of poverty keep people stuck in the pit. Hopefully, this theory will help more people understand and sympathize with the reality of being poor. Money makes money, yes, but having money also saves you money. The more money you have, the more wealth you’re able to build not only because you have extra money to save, but also because you can buy higher quality things that last, therefore spending less in the long run. Thanks, Terry Pratchett, for the simple explanation. This article originally appeared four years ago. It has been updated. The post A tale of two pairs of boots shows how the rich get richer in ways poor people simply can’t appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: MIT engineers have built a soft robotic enteroscope designed to crawl through the small intestine and help doctors diagnose and treat disorders there. The tube-like robot moves in a way inspired by snakes and carries tools for imaging, drug delivery and tissue removal. A hard-to-reach organ The small intestine is more than 20 feet (6 meters) long and about an inch (2.5 centimeters) in diameter, and it sits deep inside the body. That makes it harder to examine than the stomach or colon . Doctors most often need to evaluate bleeding, lesions and blockages there. Today, the only way to diagnose those problems is double balloon enteroscopy, where a health care worker alternately inflates and deflates two balloons to propel the scope. The process is slow and laborious. The MIT team wanted an enteroscope that is easier to control and moves faster through the intestine. Traverso said the aim is to evaluate the 20-to-25-foot (6-to-7.6-meter) segment in a more automated way. How it slithers forward A snake steers by contracting muscles on one side of its body, then the other. To mimic that, the researchers designed multifunctional actuators that control the robot’s movement. Each actuator has four chambers that can be inflated in different combinations, making the tube extend or bend in any direction. Adjusting the air going into those chambers lets operators “tune the direction that the robot is moving in,” Traverso said. The head and tail segments carry extra anchoring balloons that take turns inflating and deflating to help the robot inch forward. Those segments are covered with patterned sleeves inspired by kirigami, an origami variant that adds cuts to the folds. The coatings lie flat until the balloon beneath them expands and stretches them, which makes three-dimensional kirigami needles pop out. Like the scales of a snake, the needles give the robot more traction on the slippery intestinal lining. Traverso’s lab has used the same approach for shoe soles that grip better and for stents that can temporarily lodge in the esophagus and release drugs. Graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran, a lead author, said the sleeves let the robot gain traction at specific spots without overstretching the delicate tissue. Tools and early tests The robot is tethered by a cable to external controllers, and an operator can steer it through narrow passages and around tight corners . It is designed to enter the body through either the mouth or the rectum. Its tools include a camera for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery and clips that can take tissue biopsies or remove polyps. Traverso said the robot lets doctors “take a biopsy or remove it” if they find a small polyp. In animal studies, the robot traveled about 6.5 feet (2 meters) through the small intestine. The team also demonstrated the drug sprayer, tissue clips and camera. The researchers are now improving the navigation systems and testing the approach for additional small intestine applications. Traverso is a mechanical engineering professor at MIT, a gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and an associate member of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. The paper’s lead authors are Binbin Ying, a former MIT postdoc now at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Jebran and former MIT research scientist Sahab Babaee. The research appears in Science Robotics , with MIT’s Giovanni Traverso as senior author.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Reading Time: 3 minutes Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Replacing a car is a big decision. Replacing two familiar journeys can be a smaller, more useful experiment. An e-bike may suit a trip to work, a grocery pickup, or a visit to the library without needing to handle every journey in your week. The starting question is not “How far can this bike go?” It is “Which journeys can I repeat comfortably, legally, and with a workable backup?” This checklist helps turn that question into a practical plan rather than a promise about distance, money, or carbon savings. 1. Define the two trips you want to replace Look at an ordinary week and choose journeys you currently make by car. Start with predictable destinations, manageable loads, and flexible arrival times. An appointment with no margin for delay is probably not the easiest first attempt. Be clear about counting: an outward journey and its return are two one-way trips, but one round-trip outing. Write down which definition you are using. Two bike rides do not necessarily replace two car journeys if someone still drives the same route to collect you or your shopping. 2. Find the calmer route, not just the shortest Compare a cycling map with your knowledge of local streets. Look for lower-traffic connections, suitable crossings, and routes where you feel comfortable managing the bike. A small detour may be worthwhile if it avoids a difficult junction. Inspect the awkward details: where does a bike lane end, how do you cross a busy road, and is the destination entrance accessible? Check current local rules for your bike’s class and the roads or paths you plan to use. An app’s suggested route is not proof that access is legal or conditions are suitable. 3. Budget door-to-door time Allow time to unlock the bike, load bags, negotiate crossings, park, and get ready at your destination. Do not base your schedule on the motor’s assistance cutoff or a brief top-speed reading. Neither tells you the average speed of an entire journey. Try the route without an important deadline. Record the complete travel time and how it felt, then add a buffer appropriate to your schedule. 4. Plan battery use for the whole outing Include the return leg, any errands, and a reasonable detour. Advertised maximum range is not a dependable prediction for your route. Hills, wind, temperature, assistance level, load, battery condition, and other factors can change consumption. Begin with short, familiar rides and note battery use under your own conditions. Leave a conservative reserve rather than planning to arrive empty. If charging at work is part of the plan, confirm permission and a suitable location first. Follow the bike and battery manufacturer’s charging instructions; do not assume any available charger is compatible. 5. Solve parking and carrying before leaving Know where you can lock the bike at both ends. Check whether the parking arrangement works with the frame, your lock, and the property’s rules. If stairs or lifting are involved, assess whether you can manage the bike safely before relying on that access. Pack a realistic load for a practice ride. Secure bags so they cannot interfere with steering, wheels, or braking, and respect the bike’s and rack’s stated limits. Check tire condition and pressure, brakes, lights, and load security before departure. A lighter shopping trip may be a better starting point than a weekly household shop. For a practical example focused on weekend outings, FavoriteBikes’ guide to planning e-bike errands covers stop order, bags, cargo balance, and battery margin. Adapt those planning ideas to the trips you actually want to replace. 6. Decide when not to ride Choose your fallback before you need it. Transit, rescheduling, a lift, or using the car may be appropriate when conditions exceed your ability or the bike’s limits. Check transit rules in advance, including restrictions on e-bikes, batteries, and available carrying space. Rain, darkness, strong winds, snow, and ice can change the decision. Clothing and equipment do not make every route safe, and motor assistance does not remove traction or braking risks. Avoid an unsuitable route rather than treating two weekly trips as a target that must be met regardless of conditions. 7. Keep a simple two-week record For each attempt, note the journey replaced, door-to-door time, battery use, load, conditions, and any difficulty. Include the days you chose not to ride. Those decisions help reveal whether the plan works beyond an unusually easy day. If you compare costs, distinguish avoided fuel or parking from car expenses you still pay, and include relevant bike costs. Do not assign a fixed emissions saving to every ride: the result depends on the vehicle journey actually displaced and the comparison being made. Keep the routes that fit your life, revise the difficult ones, and leave room for other transport. The useful outcome is a repeatable choice—not a perfect score or a commitment to give up the car. The post Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: People sometimes say that dogs and their owners look alike. British photographer Gerrard Gethings took that idea a step further, finding human lookalikes for 25 dogs and photographing them in strikingly similar poses. The results are hilarious. From matching hairstyles to nearly identical expressions, some portraits look so convincing you’d swear the humans and dogs are related. Take Monica and Reggie, the pair featured in this article’s lead photograph. Reggie is a Chow Chow with a plush coat and a distinctive blue tongue. Monica has a similar hair color, but her bright blue tongue completes the illusion. Photo credit: All images used with permission of Gerrard Gethings – Henry looks remarkably similar to Hope the dog sporting windblown hair. Finding the perfect human match wasn’t easy The portraits were created for Do You Look Like Your Dog? , a memory card game published by Laurence King in 2018. The game features 25 pairs of human and canine lookalikes, with players challenged to find the matching faces. To put the collection together, Gethings first turned to social media to find dogs with distinctive features. Then came the harder part: finding humans who looked like them. Only two of the 25 humans actually owned their canine counterparts. The others were recruited specifically because they resembled a particular dog. Caspar has a fluffy face and a closely trimmed body, left, and Charlotte rocks a pair of pigtails, right. Telling someone they look like a dog Sometimes, that meant approaching strangers. In an interview with The Guardian , Gethings shared that he kept an eye out for potential matches wherever he went, including parks and buses. Sophie has jet black hair and stylish bangs, left, and Percy has a strong opinion, right. He had to find tactful ways to approach people, explain that they reminded him of a particular dog breed, and ask whether they’d be willing to pose for the portrait. “I’ve been taking photographs for a long time, so [I] am well versed in administering dubious compliments,” Gethings told The Guardian . “Without exception, people reacted positively,” he added. Fluffy Buddy the Bichon Frise, left, and Jessica with pearls and a pink sweater, right. One of those chance encounters was Jessica, a woman Gethings spotted walking through a London park. Her short, fluffy white hair reminded him of Buddy, a Bichon Frise he had already photographed. As Gethings told Artsy , finding 25 convincing pairs was challenging. He wasn’t just looking for people who vaguely resembled dogs. Each pair needed to look different from the others, and the similarities had to be obvious enough for children playing the matching game to recognize them. Josh with a fashionable beard, left, and Rupert with… a fashionable beard, right. Getting the perfect photograph took some extra work Once he found the right people, a little styling helped bring out the resemblance. For Henry and Hope, Gethings used fans to make their long hair blow in similar directions. Monica was given blue slushies and lollipops to help her tongue match Reggie’s naturally blue one. Emma with dreadlocks, left, and Ralph with corded fur, right. Other comparisons relied on smaller details. Emma’s dreadlocks resembled the corded fur of Ralph, a Hungarian Puli. A makeup artist also gave her bright pink lips to match the dog’s tongue. In a 2021 interview with Adopt a Pet, Gethings explained that different breeds respond to different things, including food, movement, and even sound. Rather than trying to make a dog produce a particular expression, he works with the animal until the right moment comes along. Benji, left, and Harper, right, both have the spiky hair look down. Gethings isn’t immune to the comparisons himself. People have said he resembles his own Border Terrier, Baxter . Apparently, even the photographer behind these portraits has a canine lookalike of his own. You can find more of Gethings’ work on his website: gerrardgethings.com The post A photographer found dogs their human lookalikes. The matching portraits are hilariously convincing. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia Hyderabad is facing a serious water crisis. One of its main reservoirs has dropped to just 13%, and 6,000 water tankers are being booked every day. But what if the solution lies in a simple idea that helped Chennai fight its own water crisis? In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something alarming. His tap water had turned salty because falling groundwater levels allowed seawater to seep in. Chennai received plenty of rainfall, but much of that water was going to waste. Instead of waiting for someone else to act, he began promoting rainwater harvesting. His idea was simple: collect rainwater from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces, filter it, and allow it to recharge underground aquifers. He cycled door to door, convincing residents to adopt the system. Many dismissed his efforts. But he persisted. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting mandatory in buildings. Groundwater levels reportedly rose by nearly 20 feet, helping Chennai improve its water security. For around 15 years, the city benefited from this approach. But there was a problem. Poor maintenance, clogged filters and neglected recharge pits weakened many systems. When Chennai faced another severe drought in 2019, the city once again came dangerously close to running out of drinking water. Today, Chennai is exploring solutions such as sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems to strengthen its water resilience. The lesson? Rainwater harvesting isn't just about installing systems. It's about maintaining them, protecting groundwater and making every drop count. With Hyderabad facing mounting water stress, could Chennai's experience offer a way forward? Should Hyderabad make rainwater harvesting a bigger priority?
