Ο πατέρας του ετοίμαζε τις βαλίτσες του για ένα ταξίδι αποστολής στην Κένυα, όπου ήταν εθελοντής με την Kenya Relief , έναν ιατρικό οργανισμό που διευθύνει ένα scho…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old. ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient. “Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request. Volunteers with the All The Same Organization Reaching Title I families across the country Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season , the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods. ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over. Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.” Cultural Surprises Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for. Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.” Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost. ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.” A classroom, and what came after After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School. When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away. “Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote. Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit. Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org . Vivian Ho, founder. The post Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Πολλές από αυτές τις πόλεις r…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the deep South to colonial New England, certain U.S. locales have developed chilling reputations for reports of apparitions and other paranormal activity. Long shadows have been cast by histories steeped in calamity, and stories abound of restless souls condemned to cemeteries and peevish poltergeists with bones to pick. Many of these cities relish their notoriety, with multiple laying claim to the title of most haunted in the country. We detail a few of them below, but whether you use this list as a roster of places you dare not enter or as a resource for your next vacation, proceed with caution: We can’t promise that reading our roundup won’t summon the spirits mentioned within it. Savannah, Georgia Glen Richard—iStock/Getty Images Plus Savannah offers all the charm of the South and all the unease of a Southern Gothic novel — if you know where to look. Lurking amid the oak-lined streets and majestic mansions are specters borne of centuries of tragedy (or so the story goes). Founded in 1733, the city played major roles in the Revolutionary and Civil Wars and was ravaged by several yellow fever outbreaks in the 1800s. The souls lost in those events are said to haunt Savannah’s historic cemeteries and buildings. “Visitors and locals alike report unexplained phenomena across Savannah: sudden cold spots, shadow figures, voices, apparitions, and objects moving without cause,” claims local hotel Bellwether House, which was built in 1876. “Ghost sightings aren’t confined to one building — they’re woven into the city itself.” Even its own chamber of commerce boasts its reputation as “the most haunted city in America” (a title New Orleans also claims). Check out 10 of the spookiest places in Savannah. Atchison, Kansas DonsESLAdventure—iStock Editorial/Getty Images Plus Known for being the birthplace of Amelia Earhart , Atchison’s other claim to fame is its purported paranormal activity. Situated on the Missouri River, it’s home to the infamous Sallie House . Legend has it that after a young girl named Sallie died there during a failed appendicitis operation in 1905, her ghost stuck around. Though locals had long considered the abode haunted, the story truly took hold in 1993 when a couple moved in and began experiencing ominous phenomena — including a fire, objects moving around on their own, and unexplained scratches. Other eerie sites in Atchison (called “America’s most haunted town” by its tourism department) include the McInteer Villa , an 1889 Victorian mansion that’s elicited reports of supernatural occurrences; the Rose Trunk Building , where visitors have claimed they sensed an unseen presence; and Benedictine College, said to be haunted by the spirits of monks who founded it over 150 years ago. New Orleans, Louisiana lightphoto—iStock/Getty Images Plus Welcome to New Orleans, a 308-year-old city rife with historical trauma. Its early days were marked by violence and sorrow, which continued into the 19th century as slavery, the Civil War, and several disease outbreaks took their toll. A merging of West African spiritual practices and Catholicism gave rise to its distinct voodoo tradition , and today, “the line between the living and the dead often feels surprisingly thin,” per the city’s tourism department. If you’re looking for a hair-raising time, you should certainly visit the French Quarter. Book a stay at the Andrew Jackson Hotel — believed to be haunted by five boys who perished there in a fire when it was a boarding school — or dine at Antoine’s Restaurant, reportedly home to 19th-century spirits who peer out from the bathroom mirrors. The ghost of author William Faulkner is said to remain in the rooms he rented in the neighborhood, which have since been converted into a bookstore called Faulkner House Books. Learn about more haunted places in New Orleans. Salem, Massachusetts AndTheyTravel—iStock Editorial / Getty Images Plus Salem’s dark history has seemingly cast a spell over the colonial New England town. The area’s notorious witch trials saw around 200 people accused of witchcraft in the 1690s. About 30 were found guilty and at least 19 were put to death. Today, this chilling past resurfaces in reports of ghost sightings and other supernatural phenomena. Proctor’s Ledge , the trials’ primary execution site, is said to be haunted, with visitors reporting cold spots, incandescent orbs, and a disembodied voice, per Ghost City Tours. The Joshua Ward House , built on the site where George Corwin — High Sheriff during the witch trials — once lived, is also the stuff of legend: An accused man named Giles Corey is rumored to have cursed Corwin and the town of Salem with his final breath during his execution. At the Old Burying Point Cemetery , established in 1637, condemned souls are believed to be responsible for mysterious shadows, noises, mist, and an overwhelming sense of despair. Anoka, Minnesota Officially known as “the Halloween Capital of the World,” Anoka is rich with tales of the paranormal. Reportedly haunted buildings include the Anoka State Hospital , a psychiatric institution that opened in 1900; Colonial Hall, where furniture is said to move around inexplicably after dark; and the old Anoka library, with a known history of “books flying off of shelves,” per local outlet HometownSource. The Anoka County Historical Society, which formerly used the library as its headquarters, offers guided ghost tours that are “60% history, 40% folklore” and based on real stories from the people who live and work in the city’s buildings. Virginia City, Nevada NNehring—E+/Getty Images “To say everything is haunted in this old mining town is not too far from the truth,” proclaims Virginia City’s tourism department. The locale topped the ranking in the 2026 Spookiest Cities Report , a playful analysis by home security company Vivint. The ranking used seven measures, adjusted for population: haunted places, ghost sightings, funeral services, haunted houses, psychics and astrologers, spiritual shops, and spooky Google search volume. Visitors can explore eerie places like the Gold Hill Hotel, Nevada’s oldest, where rumors persist of children’s ghosts running the halls, or bring home a bottle of Cemetery Gin, the city’s own distilled spirit. This month — dubbed Hauntober — one of the area’s top ghost experts is leading paranormal investigations at the historic St. Mary’s Art Center, which was originally a hospital and is known as one of Virginia City’s most haunted buildings. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania pabradyphoto— iStock/Getty Images Plus The Civil War’s Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 resulted in over 50,000 casualties, and many believe that the spirits of the soldiers who died on the battlefield remain there, reliving the brutal conflict. For over 100 years, visitors and locals have reported “phantom footsteps, ghostly drumbeats, and echoes of musket fire and cannon blasts,” per History . Other spots in the city, widely known as one of the country’s most haunted places , have their own eerie history tied to the war. The Jennie Wade House Museum commemorates, and is said to be possessed by, the only civilian killed in the battle. Visitors have claimed to hear whispers, feel cold spots, and see Wade’s ghost floating through the rooms. Those daring enough to walk into the Sachs Covered Bridge — where a trio of Confederate soldiers were executed for impersonating Union troops — may encounter three disembodied heads or feel phantom fingers tapping their shoulders.

Και μοιράζονται μερικές υπέροχες εικόνες και βίντεο στη διαδικασία. Μια νέα μελέτη από το Κέντρο Χάρβαρντ και Σμιθσόνιαν…
items.descriptionOriginal: What happened after the Big Bang? A team of physicists, harnessing the James Webb and Nancy Grace Roman space telescopes, are working to visualize the answer to that question using a novel computer simulation called Lumina. And they’re sharing some pretty stellar images and videos in the process. A new study out of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics introduces Lumina, which provides an unprecedented look at how the universe may have formed. The simulation harkens back to the nascent universe, from the dark ages that followed the Big Bang through the next 2 billion years of cosmic evolution. “The early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” lead author Oliver Zier said in a statement , crediting the James Webb scope. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.” Lumina collaboration A visualization of hydrogen re-ionization Those predictions focus on how the first galaxies, stars, and other cosmic structures were able to form amid a period of total darkness. Per a press release from MIT, the effect of the Big Bang was such that no light or radiation could pass through the “shroud” of neutral hydrogen created by the rapid expansion event. Eventually, however, two massive transformations occurred: the re-ionization of hydrogen and the re-ionization of helium. Hydrogen re-ionization refers to the era when the first stars were able to emit enough ultraviolet light to strip the neutral hydrogen of its electrons, preventing it from absorbing photons and thus “allowing light to travel freely.” Similarly, helium re-ionization refers to the breaking apart of neutral helium via high-energy light, something thought to have been fueled by supermassive black holes. The simulation captures these two essential processes in detail for the first time. Lumina collaboration A visualization of helium re-ionization “Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations,” study co-author Mark Vogelsberger said in the press release. He added the detail is unparalleled: “Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this. The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.” Looking ahead, the team is making Lumina available to the scientific community to compare its simulations with real-world snapshots taken by new and future telescopes and tell a more complete story of how the first galaxies, stars, and structures of the universe may have formed. items.descriptionOriginal: Bengaluru has a strange paradox: a city that floods every monsoon still struggles with water shortages. Watching its lakes disappear beneath concrete and waste, Harsha Tej decided to do something about it. He quit his job, picked up a shovel and began restoring the water bodies that once gave the city life. Through the BlueDot Foundation, Harsha has helped restore 18 lakes across Karnataka and plant more than 1.5 lakh native trees. From clearing invasive growth to rebuilding habitats, his work goes beyond beautifying lakes. Healthy lakes can support wildlife, help recharge groundwater and improve the landscape’s ability to manage rainwater. For Harsha, every restored lake brings Bengaluru a step closer to the city he remembers, where nature and urban life coexist. His journey shows how one person’s determination can inspire meaningful environmental change, one lake at a time. Can restoring our lakes help build a more water-secure Bengaluru? #WaterConservation #SolvedInIndia #KarnatakaLakes #GroundwaterRecharge #BengaluruLakes #LakeRestoration #Bengaluru #TheBetterIndia

items.title: Από ένα πρόβλημα ταξινόμησης του 1972 στο DIGIPIN: Η ιστορία πίσω από τους 6-ψήφιους κωδικούς PIN της Ινδίας
items.titleOriginal: From a 1972 Sorting Problem to DIGIPIN: The Story Behind India’s 6-digit PIN Codes
items.description: Μια επιστολή για επιστήμονες στον ερευνητικό σταθμό Maitri της Ινδίας στην Ανταρκτική φέρει τον ίδιο κωδικό PIN με το Panaji , 403001, επειδή το πολικό ταχυδρομείο ταξιδεύει μέσω του Εθνικού Κέντρου Πολικής και Ωκεανικής Έρευνας στο Vasco στη Γκόα. Η ιδιορρυθμία δείχνει πόση δουλειά κάνουν οι έξι αριθμοί για τα ταχυδρομεία 1,64 lakh που λειτουργεί σήμερα η India Post και την ιστορία αυτού…
items.descriptionOriginal: A letter for scientists at India's Maitri research station in Antarctica carrie the same PIN code as Panaji , 403001, because polar mail travels through the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research at Vasco in Goa. The quirk shows how much work six numerals do for the 1.64 lakh post offices that India Post operates today, and the story of that code begins with a sorting problem more than 50 years old. A country of similar place names At Independence in 1947, India had 23,344 post offices, mostly in cities, but the network had to keep pace with a growing country. The Postal Index Number, introduced on 15 August, 1972, aimed to ease the sorting and delivery of mail in a land where different places often share the same or similar names and letters arrive in a wide variety of languages. The idea came from Shriram Bhikaji Velankar, an additional secretary in the Ministry of Communications and a senior member of the Posts and Telegraphs Board. Velankar also wrote Sanskrit poetry, received the President's Award for Sanskrit in 1996, chaired the Indipex stamp exhibition in New Delhi in 1973, and retired from government service on 31 December, 1973. What each of the six digits tells you The length follows from the hierarchy of the code, which gives one digit to the zone, one to the sub-region, one to the sorting district, and three to the delivery post office. The first digit names one of eight regional zones, running from 1 for Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to 8 for Bihar and Jharkhand, while 9 belongs to the Army Postal Service. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times /AI-Generated collage) The second digit narrows the zone to a sub-region, and the third, read together with the first two, marks a sorting district headquartered at the main post office of the largest city in the area. Goa's 403 carves out a small piece of the 40 to 44 band that otherwise belongs to Maharashtra. The final three digits identify the delivery office, and a busy office that splits in two receives the next available code. Each PIN maps to exactly one delivery post office, which receives the mail for every sub-office and branch office in its jurisdiction. A single PIN code can therefore cover a cluster of villages, and two neighbouring delivery offices share only their first four digits. The same code at the edges of the map The structure holds even at altitude, where the post office in Hikkim, a Spiti Valley village , stands at 4,400 metres and closes for six months each winter when snow cuts off the settlement. Its code, 172114, places it in Himachal Pradesh through the prefix 17, and the office ranks among the highest in the world. The floating post office on Dal Lake began as a postal boat in 1953. It belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. Photograph: ( Lifeandtrendz ) The system also reaches Dal Lake in Srinagar, where the floating post office , which began as a postal boat serving lake communities in 1953, belongs to the same national network as any city head post office. The ninth zone serves a different kind of address, because the Army Postal Service runs field post offices serving the Army, Navy and Air Force across the country. The 2017 Salute a Soldier campaign, organised by India Post and the Postcrossing Society of India in Bengaluru, directed postcards of thanks to around 1,000 Army units. Why six digits still matter The model has a precedent abroad, because the United States introduced its Zone Improvement Plan code on 1 July, 1963, when letters passed through about 17 sorting stops. India followed nine years later with a hierarchy of its own, and its relevance remains clear whenever someone orders food or a parcel online. India Post has since added DIGIPIN, a 10-character code developed with IIT Hyderabad and ISRO that identifies a 4 m by 4 m square, and it complements the six-digit code rather than replacing it. The PIN still tells a sorter which zone, district and office should handle a letter, while DIGIPIN tells a delivery person which doorstep to find. Anyone can check a code using the lookup on India Post's website, and no PIN begins with 0, because the nine zones run from 1 to 9. Taken together, the digits turn an address into a route. A PIN such as 403001 tells a sorter that the mail belongs to the western zone, Goa's sorting district and the Panaji head office, and it does so without a word of any local language. That efficiency, which began on 15 August, 1972, still reaches from the largest cities to the highest hamlets. Sources ' Government expands postal network with 10,170 post offices over last 11 years ': by All India Radio News, Published on 10 December, 2025 ' What is DIGIPIN, India's new high-tech address system from Dept of Posts? ': By The Week, Published on 31 May, 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: People are drowning in eco-friendly swag—cloth tote bags, reusable water bottles, recycled notebooks, sustainable hotel toiletries, and on and on—distributed by organizations and companies eager to demonstrate their environmental bona fides. What might be even more sustainable than manufacturing and distributing all these eco-friendly products is to just…stop. The trouble is that consumers have trouble giving brands credit for such restraint, a quirk of human psychology that researchers dub “sustainable additive bias” in a new paper. “Companies that genuinely try to take eco-friendly actions, such as reducing packaging or promotional giveaways, are often not rewarded,” says study team member Linda Lemarié , associate professor of marketing at Audencia Business School in France. “What we don’t see is hard to take into consideration, and reduction leaves nothing visible, even though it’s often the best strategy from an environmental standpoint.” In the paper, Lemarié and her colleagues conducted nine different studies to demonstrate how this bias works—and what companies can do about it. The studies included a field experiment in which hotel guests rated the sustainability of the room they had stayed in, a lab experiment in which business school students chose gifts to hand out to trade show attendees, and seven online investigations in which a total of more than 2,900 participants were asked to evaluate complimentary hotel toiletries, hair care sets, music festival welcome bags, and other collections of products. Overall, the studies show that consumers see businesses as more sustainable when they provide more eco-friendly items rather than when they remove unnecessary ones—even though subtracting can lead to true: Information that confirms your beliefs...or information repeated over and over? “We were first surprised by the robustness and consistency of the effect across different contexts and with different metrics,” Lemarié says. For example, study participants judged a hotel room stocked with a large selection of eco-friendly toiletries as more sustainable than a room with a more modest set of eco-friendly products. They also judged a limited-edition tea box to which eco-friendly tea filters had been added as more sustainable than one from which they had been removed. “Then we were also surprised by the bias’s resistance to knowledge,” Lemarié says. When items weren’t labeled as being environmentally friendly , participants identified bundles with more items as being less sustainable than those with fewer. “This means that people do indeed correctly associate ‘addition with ‘less environmentally friendly.’” But when the question of sustainability comes into play, people seem to use visible components as indicators of companies’ effort. The more items, the more effort, and the more effort, the more sustainability—at least, according to our imperfect brains. Several of the experiments suggest sustainable additive bias can be counteracted when companies prioritize highly recognizable items as sustainability signals (that is, a refillable water bottle counts more than biodegradable glitter). One hints that explaining when items have been removed for environmental reasons might help, too. But accomplishing this in the real world could be tricky, Lemarié says. “The question our research leaves open is how to effectively demonstrate, without appearing hypocritical or making people skeptical, that reducing elements of a product offering, and thus offering less, is a genuine effort in favor of the environment.” Source: Lemarié L. et al. “ The more, the better? The sustainable additive bias .” Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine. AI-generated.

items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο δημοσιεύτηκε σε συνεργασία με τη Vibha. Για έναν φοιτητή που επιδιώκει ένα δίπλωμα, μια πρακτική άσκηση μπορεί να είναι η γέφυρα μεταξύ αυτού που μαθαίνει σε μια τάξη και αυτού που θα κάνει τελικά στη δουλειά. Αλλά η εύρεση της κατάλληλης ευκαιρίας δεν είναι πάντα απλή. Ο Nikhil Kumar, ένας 21χρονος φοιτητής B.Tech CSE από το Punjab, είχε συναντήσει…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with Vibha. For a student pursuing a diploma, an internship can be the bridge between what they learn in a classroom and what they will eventually do at work. But finding the right opportunity is not always straightforward. Nikhil Kumar, a 21-year-old B.Tech CSE student from Punjab, had come across internships that required candidates to hold a bachelor's degree or pay fees to gain experience. After completing his diploma in 2025, he chose to pursue a bachelor's degree. The experience made him think about the barriers other diploma students might face. At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Nikhil was already putting his coding skills to use. Alongside his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, he was developing a college management system to simplify administrative work. When Vibha's Programme Management Unit (PMU) learnt about the project, it saw an opportunity to build on it. The team was working on a semester-long internship programme in which students would spend their final semester working in industry rather than attending regular theory classes. Together, they adapted the system to help colleges monitor students' progress throughout this practical training. Sukeeratpal Singh and the Vibha PMU team helped Nikhil develop Place Intern to track students' internship progress. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The project became Place Intern, a portal that brings student internship records, faculty visits and progress reports together. "I was also curious whether whatever I was building would be used in the real world," Nikhil says. The project gave him the chance to find out. With guidance from his faculty mentor, Sukeeratpal Singh, and support from Vibha's (PMU), which works with Punjab's technical education department, Nikhil helped develop his college's internship management system into a tool that could be used by other institutions. How a college project found a purpose beyond campus At Government Polytechnic College, Talwara, Singh had been encouraging students to explore technology beyond their regular coursework. In 2023, he started a student club where interested students could spend additional time learning, experimenting, and helping one another. Nikhil stood out for his willingness to take on work independently. "He was always the one who finished the work first," Singh recalls. The two began working on a college management system that could make certain administrative processes easier to handle. They planned its features, decided how it would work and tested it over several weeks. The project caught the attention of Vibha's PMU when team member Abhay Vashisht visited the college. The team was working on the policy and programme design for a semester-long internship initiative for students in technical education. As they considered how the programme would work on the ground, they began identifying possible implementation challenges, including how colleges could monitor students throughout their internships. Nikhil's understanding of the college environment, combined with the PMU's inputs on the internship programme, helped shape the portal into a tool that could support its implementation. Nikhil built the parts that store and manage information, tested the portal, put it online and kept it running. Singh helped him understand the college workflows the system needed to support, while the PMU team shared the programme requirements, developed an initial outline for the portal and worked closely with him to refine its design through testing and feedback. Place Intern brings student progress reports, faculty visits and internship records onto one platform, reducing dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions. Building the portal also meant learning how to work with the people who would use it. Nikhil showed faculty members how to use it, wrote instructions and made changes based on their feedback. He had to think about how different people would use the system and what information they needed to access. Place Intern currently helps colleges track students undertaking internships during their final semester, when they work in industry in place of regular theory classes. It does not serve as a placement portal that matches students with employers or guarantees them internships. Its four types of users each see the information they need. Faculty members can record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces, while students submit reports on their progress. The principal closely monitors the tasks faculty and students undertake, while the Directorate in Chandigarh uses dashboard access to track progress and review updates. "By bringing these records together, the portal reduces dependence on separate spreadsheets and paper-based submissions," adds Nikhil. Building the portal taught Nikhil how to create something people could actually use, and how working closely with those using it could help make it better. 'Students need to apply their classroom knowledge' For students like Nikhil, finding an internship is one part of a larger challenge: turning a technical qualification into the skills and confidence needed to enter the workforce. Mridul Dhyani, who works with Vibha's PMU in Punjab, says diploma programmes have faced challenges around industry acceptance, student retention and employability. "Students may understand technical concepts in the classroom, but they also need opportunities to apply that knowledge and become familiar with workplace expectations," he shares. For students in rural areas, finding these opportunities can be especially difficult. Colleges may have fewer employers nearby, and students may not have family or professional networks that can connect them to industries. Sukeeratpal has seen these challenges through his work in teaching and placements. Earlier, students often had to approach companies and establish industry connections themselves. Colleges also lacked a consistent way to track internships and follow students' progress. Faculty members can use Place Intern to record monthly visits to students at their internship workplaces and track their progress during practical training. "Earlier it was in the minds of the children that a diploma is enough," Sukeeratpal says. "Now our priority has become to make the students job-ready." Addressing these gaps means helping students find openings while also introducing structured internships, strengthening industry engagement, updating curricula and developing the communication and practical skills they need at work. Place Intern helps colleges keep track of students during their internships. Finding an internship is the first step, but colleges also need to know how students are progressing, whether their training is going as planned and if they are gaining useful experience. The portal is part of a larger effort to help students build the skills they need for employment. Taking a student-built portal beyond the classroom The wider effort is supported by Vibha, which works towards ensuring high-quality public education for every child. Its mission is to improve learning levels in government schools by identifying, supporting and scaling proven solutions. It works with governments, implementation partners, educators and communities to strengthen different parts of the education system, including early reading and maths, teacher training, classroom materials, technology, record-keeping and tracking progress. In Punjab, the work focuses on technical education. "The underlying approach is similar: understand where the system is falling short, work with government teams and institutions to address those gaps, and support solutions that can become part of regular practice," adds Mridul. The Programme Management Unit (PMU) helps put this approach into practice. Working alongside government departments and educational institutions, it listens to people at colleges, identifies what needs attention, helps develop solutions and sees them put to use. For Place Intern, the PMU saw how the college's existing technology project could help manage semester-long internships. The team worked with Nikhil and Singh to understand what colleges needed, adapt the portal accordingly, and test and improve it for everyday use. Through its PMU, Vibha works with Punjab's technical education department and polytechnic colleges to bridge the gap between education and employment. The aim is to make sure the tool works for the people who will depend on it. Faculty members, college leaders and department officials need to understand how it fits into their responsibilities, while students need a clear process for submitting reports and being monitored during their internships. "We just don't work towards plans," Dhyani says. "Our work starts with a plan, but it doesn't stop till we complete the loop." That follow-through matters when a solution is expected to last beyond its development. Training, feedback and institutional ownership can determine whether a new system becomes part of everyday practice or remains a one-off project. How a 2-week maths course became part of a bigger effort Alongside efforts to help students find internships, the wider initiative has also focused on making classroom learning more relevant to their needs. Across 91 government polytechnic colleges in Punjab, the wider initiative has reached 5,921 students in FY 2026, with semester internships introduced in six courses. These numbers reflect the initiative's combined work across several interventions, not Place Intern alone. Some of the changes began with a simple question: what were students struggling with in the classroom? When mathematics emerged as a challenge, the team introduced a two-week bridge course to help students strengthen their basics. According to Dhyani, the results showed up the following year, when the proportion of students passing the subject rose from 16% to 31%. A two-week mathematics bridge course helped address gaps in students' foundational learning, with the reported pass rate rising from 16% to 31%. English classes saw a change, too. Instead of placing most of the emphasis on literature and grammar, the revised curriculum focused more on functional English and everyday conversations. The reported pass rate rose from 45% to 92%. Dhyani recalls that some teachers were initially hesitant about the shift, but later noticed that students were participating more actively in class. The programme also includes faculty training, entrepreneurship education and efforts to build stronger industry links. Each intervention addresses a different gap, but the approach remains the same: understand the problem, involve the people affected and find a solution that works within the existing system. Singh has also seen how easily industry relationships can fall apart when they depend on a single staff member who later moves on. By keeping in touch with employers and sharing responsibility across staff, colleges can make these partnerships last and give students more reliable workplace opportunities. The next step: bringing colleges and employers together Place Intern has begun supporting the tracking of semester internships at the college level. Profiles for the first batch of more than 1,500 students have been uploaded, with profiles for a further batch of over 1,700 also being prepared. These figures indicate students being recorded for tracking, not that all have secured internships through the portal. The longer-term ambition is to make it easier for colleges and employers to connect. A planned statewide platform is intended to help industries share their requirements and allow institutions to identify relevant opportunities for students across polytechnics, industrial training institutes and degree colleges. For Nikhil, developing Place Intern has offered a different kind of practical learning. He has had to understand how people use technology, respond to feedback and keep a system functioning beyond its initial development. Beyond internship tracking, the wider initiative is working to improve functional English, strengthen industry connections and help students develop practical skills for the workplace. Singh sees the project as a reason to give students more room to experiment, with faculty members providing the guidance needed to turn an idea into something useful. The next test is whether these systems can become part of everyday institutional practice, making it easier to monitor internships and build stronger links between education and employment. Nikhil's experience began with developing a college management system, but working with the PMU gave the project a wider purpose. For Nikhil, the experience has meant building his own skills while working on a tool that could make the path from education to employment easier for students who follow. All images courtesy of Vibha team

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan Reading Time: 3 minutes Bhutan’s capital is transforming the flood-prone Memorial Chorten stream into a blue-green corridor that combines flood protection, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space. A new blue-green corridor is taking shape along Thimphu’s Memorial Chorten stream in Bhutan. City planners want to turn the flood-prone waterway into a safer, greener public space. The stream flows past some of the capital’s most visited landmarks. The Memorial Chorten stream is one of five key waterways identified in Thimphu’s long-term city plan . It connects the city center to the Wang Chhu River. Rapid construction and heavier rains have made the corridor increasingly prone to flooding. The stream passes near the National Memorial Chorten, a well-known Buddhist stupa in the capital. It also runs by the Royal Bhutan Police Headquarters and the Changlimithang area. Despite this central location, much of the corridor remains hard to access today. Queen Ashi Phuntsho Choden Wangchuck built the Memorial Chorten decades ago in memory of the third king. Today it stands as one of Bhutan’s most visited religious sites. Its surrounding stream corridor sees heavy foot traffic from residents and visitors alike. Flooding has become a growing concern across Thimphu in recent years. A flash flood tore through the nearby Dechencholing community in 2025. Officials say the city, originally planned for a much smaller population, now faces mounting climate pressure. Thimphu Thromde, the city’s municipal government, has now finalized a revitalization design plan for the site. The project blends engineered flood controls with nature-based solutions to build a blue-green corridor. Together, these measures aim to lower flood risk while restoring the stream’s ecological health. Planned work includes restoring riparian plants and naturalizing the stream channel itself. New retention ponds would capture stormwater before it floods nearby streets. Waste interception systems would also help keep pollution out of the waterway. New walking trails, viewing areas, and solar-powered lighting would open the future blue-green corridor to the public. Better pedestrian paths are also expected to improve safety around the stream. Recreational spaces are planned to encourage residents to spend time outdoors. Thimphu’s planned blue-green corridor will combine naturalized stream channels, stormwater retention ponds, and waste interception systems with solar-powered walking trails, viewing areas, and recreational spaces, turning a flood-prone urban waterway into a safe, accessible public amenity. Photo by Dechen Wangmo, courtesy of UNDP . Inclusive design guided much of the planning process from the start. Planners want the corridor to feel safe and accessible for women, children, and older residents. The site’s design also considered people with disabilities. The design plan came together through the Disaster Resilient Infrastructure Project. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) supported the effort. Funding came through the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, or CDRI, and its Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund. A separate ongoing initiative will help carry the design into construction. That project, backed by UNDP and the Global Environment Facility, focuses on wider urban climate resilience. Reports indicate Bhutan has allocated roughly $24 million toward related stream corridor work. That broader initiative also covers more than 30 kilometers of stormwater drains across central Thimphu. The Global Environment Facility and the Royal Government of Bhutan jointly fund the six-year effort. Together, these projects mark one of the largest urban resilience pushes in the country’s history. Engineers, landscape architects, and gender specialists all contributed to the design. Local agencies held site assessments and community consultations before finalizing plans. That collaborative process shaped decisions on everything from drainage to lighting. Officials describe the effort as one of Bhutan’s first projects to combine several goals at once. Disaster resilience, ecological restoration, and inclusive public space design all come together in a single corridor. Few urban projects in the region have attempted such an integrated approach. The project supports goals set out in Bhutan’s National Adaptation Plan. It also echoes the country’s long-term strategy for low-emission, climate-resilient development . Urban human settlements remain a key focus area under both documents. Officials hope the corridor can serve as a practical model for other Bhutanese cities facing similar flood risks and growing pressure on urban waterways. Lessons from Thimphu could soon help guide blue-green corridor projects along other rivers and streams, showing how restoring natural waterways can strengthen urban resilience while creating healthier public spaces. For a small mountain kingdom, restoring one stream could provide valuable lessons and help protect many more communities from future flooding. The post Blue-Green Corridor Transforms a Flood-Prone Waterway in Thimphu in Bhutan appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Apapang, Alang and Ahu may weigh just 150 grams each, but they have some serious frequent-flyer miles to clock. They are Amur Falcons. In November 2025, these three Amur falcons were fitted with satellite tags by scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) in Tamenglong district, Manipur, to track their epic journey from Northeast India to Africa. Every November, thousands of these tiny birds of prey take off from roosting sites in Manipur and Nagaland , cross the Indian mainland and head over the Arabian Sea. Their itinerary? Thousands of kilometres, days over open water and no airport lounges in sight. Since the Amurs have created a mini-sensation with their incredible journey, I did a short Q&A with Dr Suresh from @wii_india who leads this remarkable tracking project. Here are a few fascinating insights Q. Why do Amur Falcons migrate? A. Migration is a natural survival strategy. Many species, including the Amur Falcon, move seasonally to escape harsh weather, seek richer feeding grounds, or find suitable breeding habitats. Over evolutionary time, individuals that migrated had higher survival and reproductive success which is why migration persists in certain species even today. Q. Why is tracking their migration important? A. Tracking with lightweight electronic tags helps scientists understand the exact routes and flight paths these birds follow, the environmental factors influencing their journey, and the critical stopover sites they depend on. It also helps identify threats along the way from habitat loss to hunting and provides vital insights into how Climate Change is shifting migration patterns worldwide. Q. How do Amur Falcons survive such long flights without food or water? A. Before they begin their transcontinental journey, Amur Falcons stop over at select sites in Northeast India, especially Nagaland and Manipur. Their arrival coincides with the mass emergence of termites a rich, high-protein food source. Here, they undergo hyperphagia or intense pre-migratory fattening, building reserves that sustain them through their nonstop oceanic flights where no food or water is available. Q. Do they take breaks while crossing the sea? A. No. Amur Falcons are terrestrial birds and cannot land on water. Once they leave the Indian coast, they undertake an uninterrupted flight across the Arabian Sea, a remarkable non-stop journey covering nearly 3000 km. — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) November 17, 2025 Their journey revealed how a bird barely heavier than a smartphone can cross thousands of kilometres of open sea. It also highlighted why Northeast India is an important stopover along their migratory route. A journey tracked across continents On 11 November 2025, WII scientists fitted Apapang, an adult male, Alang, a young female, and Ahu, an adult female, with lightweight satellite transmitters weighing approximately 3.5–4 grams. The birds took flight the following day. The tracking updates were shared by Supriya Sahu, Tamil Nadu's Additional Chief Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forests, on social media. Apapang covered approximately 6,100 kilometres in six days and eight hours. Alang travelled around 5,600 kilometres in six days and 14 hours, while Ahu covered approximately 5,100 kilometres in five days before reaching the Horn of Africa. Their routes differed, but all three completed remarkable journeys across the Indian mainland and the Arabian Sea. Subsequent tracking updates placed Apapang in Tanzania, Alang in Kenya and Ahu in northern Somalia. The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements , flight durations and stopover behaviour. Why do they stop in Northeast India? The answer lies in an insect that emerges in enormous numbers after the monsoon: termites. Amur falcons breed in parts of eastern Russia, northeastern China and Mongolia before migrating south towards their wintering grounds in Africa. During their autumn journey , Northeast India provides an important opportunity to feed and build up the energy reserves needed for their demanding flight. A 2024 study published in the Journal of Raptor Research, titled Prey Species in the Diet of the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) During Autumn Passage Stopover in Northeast India , investigated what the birds eat at their stopover sites. The birds' journeys provided researchers with valuable information about their movements, flight durations and stopover behaviour. Photograph: (Bhupender Yadav-Wildlife Institute of India) Led by researchers including Suresh Kumar of WII, the team examined approximately 1,200 regurgitated pellets collected at Pangti, Yaongyimchen and Hakhizhe in Nagaland during October and November 2017 and 2018. These pellets contained indigestible remains of the birds' prey. By examining them, researchers found that two species of subterranean termites, Odontotermes feae and Odontotermes horni , formed a substantial part of their diet. The findings help explain why the birds congregate in the region. Termites provide protein and energy that the falcons convert into fat reserves before embarking on their long oceanic flight. Researchers estimated that a million falcons could consume two billion termites in just over a fortnight. A stopover that matters beyond autumn The importance of Northeast India extends beyond the autumn migration. In a second study, published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa on 26 March 2024, researchers Tapak Tamir, Abprez Thungwon Kimsing and Daniel Mize documented repeated summer sightings of Amur falcons in D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary in Arunachal Pradesh. Here is the New Year Amur Falcon Migration -Very long Q&A Part II Q1. What is the longest non-stop distance covered by these satellite-tagged Amur Falcons? A: Published tracking shows Amur Falcons can do multi-day, non-stop flights of approx. 5,600–6,000 km during the India Africa leg, depending on the individual & year. Also, peer-reviewed/technical tracking confirms their open-sea crossings can be about 2,364–3,138 km (Somalia India), typically completed in roughly 44–80 hours. Q2. Do satellite tags interfere with their flight, health, or mating? A: Properly fitted tags are designed to minimise interference, but no tag is "zero-impact.". Best practice is to keep transmitter mass very small relative to body weight and use well-tested harness designs; the recent India work has been described as using very lightweight transmitters (a few grams). However, ethical review, careful fitting, and post-deployment evaluation should be done & is being done Q3. Do jet streams or high-altitude winds help them on this journey? A: Yes winds are a major part of the "physics" that makes the journey possible. The best-documented help is from seasonal monsoon tailwinds and strong, persistent wind systems over the Arabian Sea/Indian Ocean that can provide sustained push. Q4. How many other falcons are "accompanying" these famous three? A: These famous three are just the tagged individuals we can follow in reality, Amur Falcons migrate and roost in huge aggregations, often tens of thousands to over 100,000 at key stopovers, and broader estimates discuss movements involving very large numbers of birds across the flyway. Q5. Why have these three gone to different destinations? A: It's common for individuals of the same species to winter in different areas within southern/eastern Africa. Differences can be driven by wind and weather, refuelling success and timing at stopovers, individual strategy/experience (age, condition, learned routes) etc. Q6. When will they return and what route will they take? A: In broad terms, Amur Falcons winter in Africa and then move north in late winter/early spring, reaching breeding regions in northeast Asia around May–June. Routes can differ between autumn vs spring, and tracking shows spring and autumn ocean crossings can follow different lines. Q7. Does part of the falcon's brain "sleep" during the long flight? A: We have strong evidence that some birds can sleep in flight (including unihemispheric sleep) famously shown in frigatebirds. For Amur Falcons specifically, it's not proven. Q8. How do they decide their destination, and do they return to the same places each year? A: The best-supported explanation is a mix of: Innate navigation programmes (genetically guided ) Environmental cues (winds, weather, geography, magnetic and celestial cues), learning/experience (older birds often show more consistent routes). Satellite work indicates the species follows remarkably consistent large-scale timing and corridors, even though individuals may vary. Q9. What do they eat to fuel such massive journeys? A: During the crucial Northeast India stopover, studies show they are highly insectivorous, with termites often dominant, along with other insect groups exactly the kind of high-abundance prey that allows rapid fattening before an ocean crossing. This is why protecting stopover habitats (and the insect "boom" they depend on) is so important. Q10. Is Ahu expected to move further? Why she is stationery ? A. Periods of little movement usually indicate resting or feeding in suitable habitat. This is normal behaviour and not a cause for concern Q11. How long does the GPS tag stay on the bird? A. The tag is fixed as a backpack & expected to stay for long, however this may come off from prolonged wear and tear, the tags may also stop transmitting after prolonged battery use. As told to @supriyasahuias by @sureshwii @wii_india #AmurFalconMigration video - The stopover tagging site in Manipur — Supriya Sahu IAS (@supriyasahuias) January 4, 2026 The sanctuary, in East Siang district, covers approximately 190 square kilometres and consists largely of grasslands, alongside riverine and subtropical forests. The researchers documented sightings, including one in May, that suggested the sanctuary could serve as a refuelling site during the birds' return towards their breeding grounds. From hunted birds to protected visitors The falcons' journey has also become a story of community-led conservation. In 2012, large-scale hunting of Amur falcons around Pangti village in Nagaland drew national and international attention. In response, the Wildlife Institute of India, forest departments and local communities worked to understand the birds' migration and protect their stopover sites. Tracking efforts began in 2013. Over time, communities in parts of Nagaland and Manipur became important partners in protecting the birds. The falcons, once hunted in large numbers, increasingly became a source of local pride. Their migration demonstrates how wildlife conservation depends on connected habitats and people working across regions. A bird may breed in Asia, refuel in Northeast India and spend the winter in Africa, but its survival depends on the safety of each place along the way. For the Amur falcon, the seasonal emergence of termites is more than a feeding opportunity. It is a chance to prepare for a flight across continents. Protecting the landscapes where that preparation happens is essential to ensuring the journey continues. Sources: '6,000 km in six days: How WII tracked a trio of Amur falcons across continents' : By Malavika Jayadeep,Published on 26 November 2025 'Prey Species in the Diet of the Amur Falcon (Falco amurensis) during Autumn Passage Stopover in Northeast India' : By Amarjeet Kaur, Alex Jacob, Deven Mehta, R. Suresh Kumar, Published on 13 June 2024 'D'Ering Memorial Wildlife Sanctuary, a significant flyway and a preferred stopover (refuelling) site during the return migration of the Amur Falcon Falco amurensis' : By Tapak Tamir, Abprez Thungwon Kimsing, Daniel Mize, Published on 26 March 2024

items.descriptionOriginal: P atty Spillman and her husband farm over 400 acres of corn, soybeans and wheat in central Ohio. Both have lived in the area all their lives; his family has been on the land since 1861. In 2023, a developer proposed a data center on a nearby farm. “[The community] fought them off,” she says. “But I always kind of knew that just because the one data center had left, that didn’t mean it was going to be gone forever. Someone else was going to be right on their heels.” She was right. Less than two years later, another developer started moving forward with plans for a much larger data center, located across the street from her farm. Headwaters, a Texas-based company, wanted to annex land in Pleasant Township (where Spillman lives) and nearby Jackson Township for a 300-plus acre facility in Grove City. This is a story playing out in communities across the U.S., where A.I. demands have rapidly accelerated the need for data centers, along with the extraordinary amounts of water and energy that they consume. But residents are pushing back, advocating for more community input, insisting that the data facilities cover the full cost of locating there (such as local grid infrastructure upgrades), and even calling for outright moratoriums. Patty Spillman and her husband on their land. Courtesy of Protect Grove City Crucially, these movements don’t break along party lines: Republicans, Democrats and Independents across the country are mad — and they’re working together to block development. This bipartisan push is particularly notable at a time of intense polarization. There’s not much that people from different political parties can agree on, but according to a recent poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, very few people want an A.I. data center in their community. That’s certainly true in Grove City, a Republican-leaning suburb of Columbus, where people of all parties opposed the Headwaters development. The nature of this coalition isn’t totally unprecedented, says Megan Mullin, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles. “In so many ways, data center battles look like land use battles that have come before,” she says. “Battles over housing developments, wind farms or gas pipelines — we consistently see people come together across party lines to try to keep their community looking the way it’s always looked, and to fight back against what they perceive as harmful draws on community resources.” Mullin says a big difference now is that all of these hyper-local fights are happening at once. While one or two bipartisan coalitions on a land use debate wouldn’t rise to the level of national news, hundreds of them happening simultaneously around the country does. “That allows these local disputes to be connected to something national, and it also allows concrete movement building.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] In Ohio, residents of Grove City and the surrounding townships quickly mobilized once they realized that Headwaters wanted to site a data center in their community. “We got organized,” says Jen Belt, one of the four people behind Protect Grove City , which actively opposed the development. “Most people weren’t even aware that this was a thing. We taped flyers to every home within a three-mile radius of the developer’s site. We encouraged people to come to all of the council meetings.” They also worked on gathering signatures to encourage the Grove City city council to pass a moratorium. (Pleasant Township and Jackson Township had already passed moratoriums in the first half of 2026.) Ultimately, Belt says, they gathered more than 4,000 signatures for the online petition. Their efforts worked. In June, the city council passed a one-year moratorium on data center development. But Belt and her neighbors know it is temporary, and developers will come back once the year is up. So they have put a Community Consent Amendment (CCA) on the upcoming November ballot. If passed, it will require residents’ approval before any large-scale development can break ground. (While it’s geared toward data centers, it’s written to apply to all heavy industry.) Belt, like Spillman, lives in Pleasant Township, which she calls “suburban rural.” But she scoffs at the idea that the issue doesn’t impact her just because she’s not within city limits. “This is property that will be annexed from my town into Grove City,” says Belt, a registered Democrat. “It’s literally in my backyard. So it does affect us.” Spillman, a lifelong Republican, agrees: “This is our community. This is our neighborhood, and none of us can vote on any of this, because we don’t live in Grove City proper, but we still consider Grove City our home.” Data centers have been going up in earnest for the last decade, built to support the rapid growth of the cloud. Opposition has existed nearly as long . But as A.I. usage has exploded in the last several years, the demand for data centers has rapidly accelerated as well. The post Finally, Something Americans Agree On! appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: The cool, quiet hour after dawn feels like the best time to step outside in October, yet AIIMS says pollution stays highest in the early morning until about 8:30 or 9 am. Delhi's air shows how quickly things can turn. At 4 pm on Tuesday, 20 October, the Central Pollution Control Board put the Air Quality Index (AQI) at 179, which counts as moderate. By 7 am the next day, the Air Quality Early Warning System showed 219, which counts as poor, and it forecast 342 for 22 October. The invisible lid above the city The explanation lies in physics. Normally, temperature falls with height, so air near the ground mixes and carries pollutants upwards. University of Reading researchers Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox explain that a temperature inversion reverses this, placing warmer air above colder air like a lid on a pot. Pollutants stay near the ground, and the mixing height, the level up to which they can disperse, shrinks from about one kilometre in summer to a few hundred metres in winter. The lid sits lowest after dark. Sarath Guttikunda, founder of UrbanEmissions.Info, told Frontline that in November and December the inversion height can fall below 50 metres at night and hover around 200 to 500 metres by day. As the sun climbs, the layer lifts and the smog thins, which is why the early hours feel the worst. A bowl that holds on to smoke Delhi's geography makes this even worse. The city sits in the Indo-Gangetic plains, with the Himalayas to the north and the smaller Aravalli range to the south, which help create a natural bowl. Delhi's location between the Himalayas and the Aravallis, coupled with slow winds and little rain, allows pollution to linger. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) The Himalayas block air from flowing northward, so pollution must travel across northern India before it finds an exit over the Bay of Bengal. The monsoon rains that cleanse the air from July to September have gone by October, and winds slow down. Small shifts in weather can therefore tip the balance fast. Bhandekar and Wilcox note that on 5 January, 2025, favourable winds allowed authorities to lift some restrictions, yet by 15 January calmer winds and falling temperatures forced the city's strictest curbs. Delhi had not gained more cars, factories or construction sites from one week to the next. The Centre for Science and Environment also found something similar in winter 2023, when slow winds appeared to drive the most smog episodes in six years even though stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana nearly matched 2022. Solutions that follow the weather If weather decides when pollution turns, the Reading researchers argue, policy should follow the forecast rather than chase the smog. They suggest tightening construction restrictions when inversions are predicted, even on seemingly clear days, and designing measures for the whole Indo-Gangetic plains, since many of India's most polluted cities share the same conditions. Calm winds and falling temperatures can intensify smog even without an increase in vehicles, factories or construction. Photograph: ( The Print ) Delhi's Graded Response Action Plan already lets authorities act in advance on forecasts, with curbs ranging from dust control to limits on construction and vehicle movement. The other lever sits upwind, because smoke from stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana , where farmers clear fields quickly for wheat sowing, adds to the load each October and November. Some farmers avoid it by sowing wheat directly with a Happy Seeder , spraying a waste decomposer solution on straw , or selling paddy straw for conversion into fuel pellets . What you can do this season First, treat the cool early hours as the risky ones, since AIIMS advises staying indoors at peak hours and choosing indoor exercise over outdoor runs or cycling. Second, check the AQI daily on the SAMEER app, which AIIMS recommends, and wear an N95 mask if you step out. Third, take extra care of children, older people and anyone with heart or lung conditions, whom the AIIMS advisory flags as most at risk. Fourth, skip driving once a week to trim local emissions, as AIIMS suggests. The advice does not reach everyone equally. Business Standard reports that an air purifier costing ₹12,000 to ₹15,000 is out of reach for many informal workers, and that indoor air can still hold up to 70% of outdoor PM2.5 without sealed windows and purifiers. That is why forecast-led curbs and cleaner fields matter as much as personal habits. Delhi cannot change the bowl it sits in or the chill that settles each night, but it can change what it puts into the air beneath the lid. With poor air forecast for 21 to 23 October, the next crisp, quiet dawn is better read as a warning than a relief. Sources: 1. ' Delhi's air quality slips to poor category, forecast to worsen further ': by Akshita Singh for Business Standard, Published on 21 October, 2026 2. ' How weather patterns and faraway mountains make Delhi the world's most polluted megacity ': by Ankit Bhandekar and Laura Wilcox for The Conversation (republished by Newslaundry), Published on 3 March, 2025 3. ' Delhi's Air Pollution Explained! ': by R. Ramachandran for Frontline, Published on 9 December, 2016 4. ' Delhi's annual battle with air pollution: Aiims issues health advisory ': by Barkha Mathur for Business Standard, Published on 6 November, 2025 5. ' 2023 ended on a high pollution note, says latest CSE analysis of winter air pollution levels in Delhi-NCR ': by Centre for Science and Environment for CSE (press release), Published on 4 January, 2024
