items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study Reading Time: 3 minutes A major five-year study finds that urban woodlands and mental health are closely connected, with well-kept city woods linked to fewer antidepressant prescriptions in Scotland’s poorest neighborhoods. Urban woodlands and mental health appear to move together, according to new research from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow. Scientists tracked more than 129,000 people across Scotland over five years. They found that people living close to improved woodlands used less medication for depression and anxiety. The study , published in The Lancet Planetary Health, used National Health Service prescription records alongside census data. Researchers compared people living within a 10-minute walk of an upgraded woodland to those living farther away. The gap in medication use was substantial. People near a well-maintained, welcoming woodland were 10% less likely to be prescribed antidepressants. They were also 6% less likely to need anti-anxiety medication. That pattern held even after researchers accounted for income, demographics, and other factors known to affect mental health. This is one of the largest studies of its kind linking urban woodlands and mental health outcomes. The woodland upgrades came through Scottish Forestry’s Woods In and Around Towns program (WIAT). Funding paid for new footpaths, better signage, and community events in areas that needed it most. The program specifically targeted socially and financially disadvantaged communities. These are often the places with the least access to quality parks and green space to begin with. By focusing improvements there, researchers could measure whether fixing a woodland actually changed people’s health, not just their surroundings. What makes this research especially convincing is how it tracked people over time. When someone moved closer to an improved woodland, their need for medication tended to drop. When they moved farther away, that protective effect faded. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health was strengthened with a telling finding: when people moved closer to improved woodlands, their need for antidepressants fell, and when they moved away, the protective effect faded with them. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Pexels. That detail matters. Earlier studies often compared different people living in different neighborhoods at a single moment. This approach made it hard to know whether nature improved mental health, or whether healthier people simply chose to live near woodlands already. By following the same individuals as their circumstances changed, researchers could rule out that explanation. Professor Catharine Ward Thompson, who led the study at the University of Edinburgh’s OPENspace Research Centre, said the findings offer stronger evidence on the link between urban woodlands and mental health than earlier research managed to provide. She added that the benefits may help reduce mental health inequalities across the population. Dr. Scott Ogletree, who carried out the analysis, said the project marks the first time mental health service data has been linked to a long-term national urban forestry program. He noted that relatively modest investments in local green space can meaningfully improve people’s wellbeing. Nature-based programs like WIAT, he said, can support broader efforts to improve mental health. The scale of the problem makes this evidence timely. Around one in eight people worldwide live with a mental health condition, and people in poorer communities are often hit hardest. These same communities often have the least access to high-quality woodlands and parks. Scotland’s government has pointed to this research as support for its wider environmental goals. Officials cited a target of creating 18,000 hectares of new woodland every year by 2029 to 2030. That commitment extends to urban tree planting aimed at improving air quality and quality of life. The connection between urban woodlands and mental health also fits into a broader pattern seen elsewhere, where community-driven tree planting has helped cool neighborhoods and improve public health by giving residents a direct role in restoring local green space. Programs like these suggest the benefits of investing in trees extend well beyond any single country. The research team behind the Scottish study has spent more than 20 years gathering evidence on the social value of local woodlands, working alongside Scottish Forestry and Forest Research. Their latest findings add a rigorous, long-term dataset to a growing conversation about nature-based public health policy. Funding came from the Economic and Social Research Council and the GroundsWell Consortium, a UK research partnership focused on how green and blue spaces reduce health inequalities. None of this suggests woodlands replace clinical care for depression or anxiety. What it does suggest is that a safe, welcoming patch of trees within walking distance can meaningfully shift the odds. As more cities weigh where to spend limited public money, the growing evidence on urban woodlands and mental health makes a strong case for choosing the trail over the parking lot. The post How Urban Woodlands and Mental Health are Connected, According to a Major Scottish Study appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when two generations open their doors to one another? In West Philadelphia, a small but growing program called Second Story Collective is bringing college students and older residents together through shared housing, creating unexpected friendships along the way. For Ms. Julia, a retired nursing assistant who has lived in her neighborhood for more than 50 years, welcoming 22-year-old Drexel University student Jackson Tignor into her home has brought new companionship and laughter. In return, Jackson has found more than an affordable place to live -- he's discovered a sense of belonging and a deeper connection to the community around him. Through everyday moments of shared meals, conversations, and helping hands, the program is quietly challenging loneliness, housing insecurity, and the divisions that too often separate generations. Sometimes, building a stronger community begins with something as simple as opening a door.

Η Νίκη Ράι, που είχε οργανώσει τη συγκέντρωση, ζήτησε από τους καλεσμένους της να κρατήσουν το σπ…
items.descriptionOriginal: At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, lunch was over and everyone was waiting for dessert. The thalis had been cleared, conversations had moved on, and there was only one thing left to do: bring out the kheer. Except this time, there was something unusual in the cutlery. Niki Rai, who had organised the gathering, asked her guests to hold on to their spoons instead of throwing them away. A few eyebrows went up. She had already told everyone that these were edible, but people were still understandably unsure. Then came dessert. "Now this is your biscuit," Rai told the children, handing them their dessert with the spoon. The reaction was almost immediate. The children started biting into the spoons, treating them less like cutlery and more like a crunchy snack. The adults were more hesitant, watching first to see if it really worked. Soon, however, others wanted a taste too. "It was quite a spectacle, but it was worth it," Rai recalls. The spoons had been made by Mumbai-based startup Edybites, which is trying to tackle a very ordinary problem: what happens to a disposable spoon after the few minutes it spends helping us finish a meal? Its answer is simple enough to eat. Founded by Rupesh K Sanghvi in 2022, Edybites makes edible spoons using a millet and flour-based formulation. The idea is that the spoon can become part of the meal rather than another piece of waste to be thrown away. If it is not eaten, the product is designed to naturally decompose. After 88 failed attempts, Sanghvi refined the spoon's shape, texture and sturdiness to make it practical for everyday use. But turning that simple idea into a spoon that could hold its own through a meal was another story. It had to be sturdy enough to carry food, pleasant enough to eat and practical enough to make at a price people would accept. The idea began with a spoon and a piece of khakra For Sanghvi, the thought first came during the COVID-19 lockdown. With fewer services and errands available, everyday household work suddenly meant doing much more oneself. One day, after preparing a meal and looking at a sink full of utensils, he found himself eating with his fingers because there was no clean spoon left. That brought back a familiar Gujarati food memory: khakra. "If we can finish our last meal of dal khichdi with a combination of khakra," he thought, could something similar be made in the form of a spoon? The thought stayed with him. It also connected with something Sanghvi had observed during his more than 17 years in the aviation and travel industry. Having worked in sales and business development with airlines including Malaysia Airlines, Flydubai, Malindo Air and Kuwait Airways, he had seen how much disposable material moved through a flight. Once a flight landed, used food packaging and cutlery had to be discarded. Some meal components could not be reused because of safety and airline policies, even when they had not been consumed. The edible spoons are designed to hold food during a meal and can be eaten afterwards, reducing the need for disposable plastic cutlery. For Sanghvi, that raised a broader question : could at least one small part of the meal be made differently? He initially imagined the spoon being used with yoghurt, pastries, desserts or dishes such as dal khichdi and sambar rice on flights. Aviation remains one of the sectors he is interested in, alongside hospitals, institutional catering and events. The larger idea, however, is not simply to tell people to use less plastic. It is to make the alternative convenient enough that people actually use it. Making a spoon that does not fall apart That turned out to be the difficult part. Sanghvi says he failed 88 times while developing the spoon. Each version had to be tested for its shape, size, weight, and sturdiness. It needed to be strong enough to hold food, but not so hard that eating it became uncomfortable. The formulation uses a combination of sorghum, corn flour, and wheat flour, along with other ingredients. Sanghvi says the precise recipe is proprietary, but the millet and flour-based formulation is central to giving the spoon its structure. Too much flour, and the spoon could become soggy quickly. Too much firmness, and it could become difficult to bite. The team also experimented with flavours. Chocolate emerged as one of the main variants, particularly because it pairs naturally with vanilla ice cream. Edybites offers different flavours, including chocolate, which pairs well with desserts such as vanilla ice cream. That makes dessert one of the easiest places to introduce the concept. A person may be more willing to eat a spoon after finishing a bowl of ice cream than rethink every piece of cutlery used during an entire meal. There is also a practical reason Edybites has focused on spoons rather than trying to replace every disposable food item at once. Sanghvi says other edible products, such as cups, can face challenges when they are expected to hold liquids for longer periods. With tea or coffee, for instance, the material can soften or affect the eating experience. The spoon offers a smaller, more manageable starting point. The product has a shelf life of about three months without refrigeration, with the team working towards extending it further. It is made under a contractual manufacturing arrangement, with attention to hygiene and the heating process required to form the spoon. The finished spoons are individually covered and packed in boxes designed to minimise breakage during transportation. The product also requires the relevant food safety certification, including an FSSAI licence. When the spoon reached a real dining table For Niki Rai, the real test came not in a product demonstration but at a family gathering. Rai, a learning and development professional and executive coach, had first heard about the product through a friend. She was curious but wanted to try it herself before recommending it to others. When she eventually used Edybites spoons at a Ganpati gathering, she served them alongside a regular thali and asked guests to try them with the sabzi. Later, she brought them out again with kheer. The children needed little convincing. "For kids, it was like a biscuit," she says. For adults, the experience was more about getting used to the idea. Rai says the spoon felt similar to a regular spoon and was comfortable to use, although its smaller size meant it could not hold a large quantity of food. She found it particularly suited to desserts, while children could use it for foods such as porridge too. At a Ganpati gathering in Mumbai, Niki Rai introduced Edybites spoons to guests, with children happily biting into them like biscuits after dessert. What stood out most to her was not just that the spoon was edible, but that it did not feel like a compromise. For Rai, taste was important. She also liked that the ingredients included grains such as jowar and wheat, along with fenugreek, rather than making the spoon feel like an entirely separate object that happened to be sustainable. Once the children started eating theirs, curiosity took over. The parents who had initially been apprehensive began joining in. Soon, Rai says, people were asking for extra spoons. Since then, she has continued recommending the product at events and gatherings, including while travelling. Making the sustainable choice practical There is, however, a catch. An Edybites spoon currently costs around Rs 7-8, according to Sanghvi. That is considerably more than a conventional disposable spoon, making price one of the biggest hurdles to getting people to make the switch. After all, when a plastic spoon costs a fraction of that, convincing someone to pay more for something they will eat or discard after one meal is not easy. Sanghvi has seen this play out in the conversations around the product. "However rich you are, at one point you would think, just to have a spoon, why should I pay seven rupees?" he says. That is why Edybites has not tried to rush into the mass market. Since November last year, when the startup began seeing stronger market traction, it has sold or distributed more than 5,100 spoons. For now, Sanghvi is taking a gradual route, exploring events, institutional catering, hospitals and airlines, along with markets where customers may be more willing to pay for sustainable alternatives. Edybites spoons blend sorghum, corn and wheat flour to create a sturdy yet easy-to-bite alternative to plastic cutlery. There is another irony to solve, too. The spoon is edible, but it still needs to reach the customer intact. That means packaging it carefully against moisture and breakage. Sanghvi says the team is experimenting with paper-based packaging and ways to reduce plastic without compromising the product. For a startup trying to eliminate one disposable item, using plastic to protect that alternative is hardly an ideal solution. It is a problem the team is still working through. What happens when a spoon becomes part of the meal? Perhaps the most interesting thing about Edybites is that its sustainability pitch does not end with the word "biodegradable". It asks people to rethink what they consider waste in the first place. A conventional spoon has a very short life. It may spend a few minutes carrying a bite of food before being separated from the meal and sent to a bin. Edybites is trying to stretch that experience a little further: what if the spoon itself became the final bite? At scale, that could add up. Based on an estimated 2.5-3 grams of plastic in a conventional disposable spoon, Edybites estimates that every one lakh edible spoons could potentially displace around 250-300 kg of single-use plastic. At 10 lakh spoons, that works out to roughly 2.5-3 tonnes of potential plastic displacement. These are estimates of what could be displaced if the edible spoons replace plastic ones at that scale, rather than plastic waste already avoided by the startup. For Sanghvi, however, the number is only one part of the larger picture. He is particularly interested in what happens when children encounter such alternatives early. His hope is that edible or biodegradable options could eventually find their way into school canteens, hospitals, senior-care facilities and other places where disposable cutlery is used every day. And perhaps that is where Rai's Ganpati gathering offers a glimpse of what adoption can look like. Edybites has sold or distributed over 5,100 spoons and estimates that replacing one lakh plastic spoons could potentially prevent 250–300 kg of single-use plastic waste. The children simply needed to know they could eat the spoon. Once they did, the idea stopped being a sustainability lesson and became something much more familiar: a biscuit-like treat at the end of a meal. Rai has continued recommending the spoons at gatherings since that first experience, and her reason is simple. "We've got to be a flag bearer in our own way, no matter how small that change is," she says. For now, Edybites is still figuring out how to make that small change cheaper, easier to package, and practical at a much larger scale. But somewhere between a Mumbai kitchen, 88 failed attempts and a group of children happily chomping through their spoons after dessert, the idea has found its most convincing test yet. The spoon did not end up in the bin, it ended up being dessert. All images courtesy of Edybites team

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most people moving through a train station aren’t really paying attention. They’re somewhere between where they left and where they’re going, phone out, eyes on the platform. Putting art there is an interesting bet; you’re trying to get someone to stop and look at something that might surprise and delight them, and that they had no intention of seeking out. NJ Transit has been doing this since 2019, when it launched the TRANSITional Art Project as a pilot at Newark Penn Station. Working with the New Jersey State Council on the Arts , it has since installed temporary exhibitions of murals and photography by New Jersey artists at seven more stations. The latest is now at Morris Plains Rail Station: a show called “ Tracks Through Time: Movement, History and Human Connection .” A show about the tracks themselves The subject matter has good timing. The exhibition looks at 250 years of American history through the lens of railroads , in the very stations where people still depend on those rails to get to work. It includes photography by Beyti Barbaros, murals by Jonathan Yumi, and a three-panel mural installation by Catherine Thurston. “Railroads helped to build this nation,” said NJ Transit President and CEO Kris Kolluri, “and as we mark 250 years of our shared history, there’s no better place to tell that story than in the very stations where the past and daily life intersect.” Art you don’t have to go looking for Nobody goes to a train station specifically to see art, but that might be at the heart of the reasoning for this whole project. Most people at a gallery already decided they wanted to be there. The commuter who glances up at a mural while waiting for the 8:14 didn’t, and that’s a different kind of encounter. Danielle Bursk, the New Jersey State Arts Council Director of Community Partnerships & Artist Services, put it this way: “Public art has the power to transform the places we move through every day into places where we can pause, connect , and see our communities in new ways.” The program also pays the artists. Some participants receive stipends toward the cost of developing a project in a transit space, which matters given how rarely public art comes with any budget at all. The program has now reached eight stations: Newark, Camden, Atlantic City, Trenton, New Brunswick, Summit, Rahway, and Morris Plains. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Columbia University Medical Center wanted to answer a specific question: what is the least amount of movement needed to offset the effects of prolonged sitting ? In 2023, they tested a range of options and found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy. Not a longer walk once an hour. Not standing more. The answer was as short and sweet as five minutes, every half hour. When NPR’s Body Electric ran that same challenge with more than 20,000 listeners, participants reported higher productivity and lower fatigue. Those results have real implications: adults in the United States average 9.5 hours of sitting per day, and the research linking prolonged sitting to fatigue, weight gain, back pain , and chronic disease is extensive. The five-minute walk is the most surprising and accessible finding, but there are four other adjustments, drawn from physical therapists, a biomechanist, and a professional ergonomist, that address what walking breaks alone can’t fix. For back pain: a three-dimensional spine rotation Slouching at a desk doesn’t just feel uncomfortable; it puts sustained stress on the middle section of the spine. Vinh Pham , a physical therapist, recommends a move he calls the 3D T-spine rotation. Stand and drop your right foot behind your left, about a foot apart. Hold your right arm straight up and your left arm behind you, as if shaking the hand of someone behind you. Then simultaneously drop both arms and twist toward your right foot, keeping them straight throughout. Return to the starting position, hold for two seconds, and repeat ten times before switching sides. The goal isn’t stretching in the conventional sense. It’s to get the spine comfortable with its full range of motion — side bending, backward bending, rotating — so those movements don’t cause pain when they come up in ordinary life. For eye strain: look somewhere else Digital eye strain happens when the eyes spend hours focused at close range. They turn inward to track a nearby screen, adjust their focus for short vision, and hold that position. Eye doctors say the result is often fatigue, headaches, or blurred vision. The simplest intervention is the one most people already know and skip: look away from the screen and focus on something distant. A full eye-muscle stretch goes further. That means moving your gaze deliberately through different positions to work muscles that stay locked during screen time . For restlessness: stop trying to find the right posture Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position , is direct on the idea that fidgeting is a signal, not a bad habit. It means your body needs to stop holding a static position, regardless of how ergonomically correct that position might be. Bowman and physical therapist Leada Malek , author of Science of Stretch , share a phrase common in their field: “Your best posture is your next posture.” Any position, held long enough, creates strain. The goal isn’t to find the correct one and maintain it; it’s to keep moving between positions. Sitting, standing, reclining, shifting. “Adaptive and dynamic,” as Malek describes it, and easy to move in and out of. For shoulder and neck aches: fix the monitor height first Professional ergonomist Meg Honan identifies one setup problem that causes more widespread discomfort than almost anything else: the “head down, arms up” configuration, where the screen is too low and the keyboard is too high. Bring your screen to eye level using books, a stand, or whatever is available. Lower your keyboard and mouse so you’re not shrugging to type. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, an external keyboard lets you lower your arms without losing screen height. Honan describes the head-down, arms-up position as a reliable setup for feeling “achy, sore and tired.” Getting the monitor to eye level is the single adjustment with the most downstream effect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Reading Time: 2 minutes 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today Making your home more sustainable doesn’t require expensive renovations or a complete lifestyle overhaul. In fact, some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple, and you can start making them today. From the products you use to clean your kitchen to the materials you sleep under, everyday household choices can affect the environment. If you want to reduce waste, embrace more natural materials, and make your home a little greener, here are five sustainable swaps to consider. 1. Swap Disposable Cleaning Products for Reusable Alternatives Consider how many paper towels, disposable wipes, and plastic cleaning bottles you use in a typical month. These everyday essentials can create surprising waste, especially when you replace them constantly. Instead, consider switching to washable microfiber cloths, reusable cleaning pads, and refillable spray bottles . You can also explore concentrated cleaning solutions that require less packaging and are designed to be diluted at home. These small changes can reduce household waste while helping you save money over time. 2. Choose Natural Bedding Over Synthetic Materials Your bedroom is another great place to introduce more sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Many conventional comforters contain synthetic polyester fillings derived from petroleum-based materials, which can contribute to plastic pollution. Replacing them with natural alternatives is a more environmentally conscious choice. An organic wool comforter offers a natural filling that provides warmth while allowing air to circulate and helping regulate temperature throughout the night. Wool is also renewable and biodegradable when untreated, making it an appealing option for anyone looking to reduce reliance on synthetic textiles. Your bedroom is a great place to introduce sustainable materials, especially in your bedding. Image: Home of Wool 3. Replace Single-Use Kitchen Products The kitchen is often one of the biggest sources of household waste, but it’s also one of the easiest places to make sustainable improvements. Instead of relying on plastic wrap, disposable sandwich bags, and single-use food containers, invest in reusable alternatives. Glass storage containers, washable silicone bags, and beeswax food wraps can help you cut down on unnecessary packaging. You could also swap disposable coffee pods for a reusable coffee filter or French press. Over time, these changes can noticeably reduce how much waste leaves your kitchen. 4. Switch to Energy-Efficient Lighting If you’re still using traditional incandescent light bulbs, switching to LED alternatives is a straightforward way to reduce household energy consumption. LED bulbs use significantly less electricity and generally last much longer than incandescent bulbs, so you need to replace them less often. This can help lower both your electricity bills and your home’s environmental footprint. You can also make better use of natural daylight by keeping windows unobstructed and arranging furniture to maximize available sunlight. 5. Choose Refillable Bathroom Essentials Bathrooms can quickly accumulate plastic packaging, particularly from shampoo, conditioner, hand soap, and body wash bottles. Switch to refillable products or solid alternatives, such as shampoo bars and bar soaps. Many brands now offer concentrated refills, so you can reuse existing containers instead of buying new plastic bottles every time. You might also replace disposable cotton rounds with washable alternatives and choose toothbrushes with replaceable heads to cut unnecessary waste. Start with one or two manageable swaps, build on them gradually, and you’ll soon discover that sustainable living can be both practical and rewarding. The post 5 Sustainable Swaps You Can Make Around Your Home Today appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: He’s the first Indian to win the Oskar Klein Medal, yet he still cycles to work. His story is as much about simplicity as it is about extraordinary scientific achievement. Meet Kolkata-born theoretical physicist Ashoke Sen, whose pioneering research in string theory and black hole physics has helped shape our understanding of the universe. After studying at Presidency College and IIT Kanpur and pursuing doctoral research in the United States, he returned to India to continue his scientific journey. In 2012, Sen received the $3 million Fundamental Physics Prize for his contributions to string theory. In 2026, he made history by becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the Oskar Klein Medal, recognising his influential work in theoretical physics. Despite global recognition and some of the field’s highest honours, Sen’s story reminds us that scientific greatness is measured by curiosity, dedication and the ideas we contribute, not by outward displays of success. His journey continues to inspire young Indians to pursue knowledge and push the boundaries of human understanding. Know a student who’s drawn to physics? items.titleOriginal: 'I Spent 4 Years Farming on Weekends. Here Are 7 Things to Know Before Starting Your Own Organic Farm'
items.description: Για χρόνια, ο Deepak Sabharwal γνώριζε το φαγητό σε μεγάλο βαθμό από την άλλη πλευρά του τραπεζιού. Είχε περάσει σχεδόν δύο δεκαετίες στον εταιρικό κόσμο, συνεργαζόμενος με εταιρείες όπως η General Electric (GE), η PepsiCo και η Tata. Οι μέρες του αφορούσαν συναντήσεις, αριθμούς και ανάπτυξη. Η γεωργία ήταν κάτι που περνούσε χρόνο κάνοντας τα Σαββατοκύριακα, στις φάρμες της οικογένειάς του στο Pushkar, R.…
items.descriptionOriginal: For years, Deepak Sabharwal knew food largely from the other side of the table. He had spent nearly two decades in the corporate world, working with companies such as General Electric (GE), PepsiCo, and Tata. His days were about meetings, numbers, and growth. Farming was something he spent time doing on weekends, at his family's farms in Pushkar, Rajasthan. Then one day, he noticed the pesticides being used on his own farm . Around the same time, his mother was diagnosed with cancer. The two things came together in his mind in a way he could not ignore. "I began wondering what we were really eating every day, and that was a simple but uncomfortable question to ask," he tells The Better India . That question eventually took him from boardrooms to fields. His hands-on farming journey began in 2012, while he was still working at GE, and he spent almost four years travelling to Pushkar on weekends to learn farming and experiment on his family's land. Today, he is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited . The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making produce grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers more accessible to urban families. Deepak wanted Earthy Tales to do more than sell vegetables. For the co-founder, it was about fixing a disconnect he had begun to see between the soil, the farmer, and the person eventually eating the food. Years of working closely with farmers taught him that organic farming involves much more than avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. Here are seven lessons he wishes anyone entering the space would understand. 1. Start with the soil It is tempting to begin a farming business by asking one question. What should I grow? Deepak believes there is another question that should come first. What is the condition of my soil? Today, Deepak is based in Delhi NCR and is the co-founder and CEO of Earthy Tales Organics Private Limited. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land, and finding out which chemicals may have been used there. Because for him, organic farming does not begin with a label. It begins underground. "Organic farming begins with soil, not with certification or branding," he says. A healthy farm may require compost, organic matter, mulching, natural inputs, better water management and, where appropriate, livestock integration. The aim is to move away from synthetic pesticides and fertilisers while gradually rebuilding the health of the land. That is also why he advises beginners not to convert an entire farm at once. He suggests starting with a small patch, trying a crop and observing how it performs over one or two cycles before taking the bigger plunge. After all, the soil has its own pace. A business plan cannot always make it move faster. 2. Build the whole system One of his early assumptions was that organic farming was largely about avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. He soon realised how incomplete that understanding was. Seed selection, soil health, water, compost, livestock, pest management, crop planning, harvesting, grading, storage, and transport all become part of the equation. "Natural farming is not only about not using chemicals. It is a complete system," he says. And the work does not end when the crop leaves the field. It has to be sorted, packed, and transported. Some produce will be damaged. Some will not look perfect. Some may not sell in time. All of that has a cost. For someone starting, this is an important reality to understand. You are not simply starting a farm. You are building a system around that farm. 3. Earn farmer trust Getting a farmer to change the way they have farmed for years is not as easy as giving them a training session. Deepak learnt this by working closely with farmers. A farmer cannot treat a crop as an experiment. A crop failure can mean a family's income is affected. So when someone asks a farmer to reduce their reliance on synthetic pesticides or change farming practices, the farmer needs more than promises. "Farmers do not trust speeches. They trust consistency," he adds. The aim is not only to stop using chemicals, but to gradually rebuild the health of the land. That consistency can mean repeated visits to the farm, helping identify pests, discussing what to do when a crop begins to fail , providing training and, most importantly, helping create a market for what the farmer grows. At Earthy Tales, the approach has involved working closely with farmers and supporting them in moving towards natural farming methods that rely less on synthetic inputs. The lesson is particularly important for entrepreneurs who want to work with farmers. If you want farmers to take a risk with you, you have to be willing to share some of that risk. 4. Find buyers first This was another lesson that took the co-founder time to learn. In farming, it is easy to fall in love with the idea of growing something. But a good crop does not automatically become a good business. "Natural farming must be market-linked. Otherwise, the farmer carries all the risk," he says. So before sowing, an entrepreneur needs to think about the customer. What does the customer buy regularly? What can the region grow reliably? What price is realistic? How far does the produce need to travel? Who will buy it? At Earthy Tales, he noticed that many customers first came looking for fresh fruits and vegetables. Once they developed confidence in the source, they began buying everyday staples such as atta, pulses, oils, spices, and ghee. The company was formally started in December 2018 with a focus on natural farming, farmer livelihoods, and making chemical-free food more accessible to urban families. That taught him something important about building a food business. Trust usually comes before the larger basket. A farmer may produce something excellent. But if there is no reliable buyer at the other end, the farmer still carries the risk. The market, therefore, cannot be an afterthought. It has to be part of the crop plan from the beginning. 5. Plan for uncertainty This sounds obvious, but it is one of the hardest realities for a business-minded newcomer to accept. Nature does not work according to demand forecasts. A farmer can plan for a crop, only for rain, heat, pests, or disease to change the outcome. Even when the crop does well, demand may not arrive at the same pace. Deepak remembers believing in the early days that good produce would naturally find its way to customers. "I believed that if we had good produce, the rest would follow," he says. "But food does not work like that." A crop arrives when it is ready, not when the customer wants it. It also creates a risk of wastage. Produce can be rejected because it is bruised, oddly shaped, or simply because there is more of it than the market needs that week. For a new entrepreneur, planning for unpredictable harvests and demand is essential. Crop cycles, storage and transport need to be flexible enough to handle surplus produce or unexpected delays. The more fragile the system, the more one bad season can hurt. 6. Know your numbers There is a natural temptation to think that a business built around a good cause will eventually work itself out. The co-founder has learnt otherwise. Organic farming can involve higher planning requirements, uncertain yields, wastage, packaging costs, logistics and working capital. If these numbers are ignored, even a business with the right intentions can struggle. "You cannot build a farmer-first business if the business itself is not financially sustainable," he says. That does not mean reducing farming to profit margins. It means understanding that farmers cannot be supported by a business that keeps losing money. For him, the lesson is to calculate what each sale really costs, from sourcing and packaging to transport and wastage, before deciding whether the business can grow. The goal is to find a balance where the customer gets trustworthy food, the farmer gets a fairer return, and the business remains strong enough to keep going. 7. Give it time Perhaps the biggest investment an aspiring organic farmer needs is not money. It is patience. Soil may take time to recover . Farmers may take time to trust a new method. Customers may take time to change their buying habits. And a young business may take years before its systems begin to settle. Before investing heavily, he advises testing the soil and water, understanding what was previously grown on the land. The co-founder knows this personally. His own journey began with weekend trips to Pushkar while he was still working full time. For almost four years, he travelled between his corporate job and the farm, slowly learning what it meant to grow food. A good farm needs more than good crops "Patience is not optional in this business. It is part of the model," he says. That patience is also needed when things go wrong. A farmer may have a poor harvest. A crop may not sell. A transition may take longer than expected. A customer may question the price. The temptation is to look for a shortcut. But Deepak's experience has taught him that there are very few shortcuts when you are trying to change something as fundamental as how food is grown. Deepak's journey from corporate offices to farming has given him a broader view of an organic farming business. Growing crops without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers is only part of the work. The rest is making sure farmers earn a fair return, produce reaches customers and the business can keep going. For him, Earthy Tales is an attempt to bring soil health, farmer livelihoods and consumer wellbeing together. And for anyone thinking of starting an organic farming business, the question goes beyond how much they can grow. It is whether they can build a system in which the soil, the farmer and the customer all have a reason to stay. All pictures courtesy Deepak Sabharwal.

items.titleOriginal: Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It
items.description: Σε πολύ λίγες εβδομάδες, η Jackie Jantzi κάθεται στις συνεδριάσεις της σχολικής επιτροπής στο Akron του Οχάιο, κρατώντας σημειώσεις στο φορητό υπολογιστή της. Στη συνέχεια, εκπονεί μια περίληψη του τι συνέβη, η οποία θα δημοσιευθεί στο Διαδίκτυο, δωρεάν για όλους. Η Jantzi εργάζεται εκεί για τον τοπικό ειδησεογραφικό ιστότοπο Signal Akron, αλλά δεν είναι επαγγελματίας ρεπόρτερ. Είναι μια από τις εκατοντάδες κατοίκους της πόλης…
items.descriptionOriginal: E very few weeks, Jackie Jantzi sits in on school board meetings in Akron, Ohio, taking notes on her laptop. Afterward, she polishes a summary of what happened, to be published online, free for anyone to read. Jantzi is there working for local news website Signal Akron , but she isn’t a professional reporter. She’s one of hundreds of city residents deployed by the news outlet to record what happens at local government meetings, through a program called Documenters . The write-ups they produce don’t just help the news outlet cover far more than would otherwise be possible with its staff of six reporters; they also create a public record where Akronites can follow the nitty gritty of the local decisions shaping their community. “National politics feels like you have zero power, you know? It just feels so big and out of your hands,” Jantzi says. “But any sort of civic engagement, like Documenters or even getting to know your neighbors, gives you a little bit of power locally.” As thousands of local news outlets have shrunk or shuttered , many Americans have lost reliable sources of information about municipal budget negotiations and school board votes. In their stead, national news has comprised a larger share of the public’s media diet, drawing attention to partisan divides and widening political polarization. By spotlighting community level issues, local news sources are finding ways to invigorate interest around what’s happening in their communities, helping people to refocus on public decision-making in their own backyards — which tends to fall less along the national red-blue divide. A Documenter on assignment in Chicago. Credit: City Bureau “When people have a chance to be able to talk about politics with nuance, to talk about how decisions that are being made in government affect their neighborhoods and communities, it drastically changes the types of conversations that folks have about things like health care, like access to food, like immigration,” says Max Resnik, who is helping to grow a network of 25 local Documenters programs across the country. Local news has suffered for the last three decades amid competition for attention — first from cable news, then the internet and now social media, explains Johanna Dunaway, a professor of political science at Syracuse University. As revenue dropped, outlets invested less in their newsrooms, leaving diminished staff capacity to report on towns and neighborhoods. In 2002, for every 100,000 Americans, there were 40 journalists covering local news . Today, the rate works out to 7.8. In many places, entire outlets have disappeared. Almost 40 percent of local newspapers have closed since 2005, and about one in seven Americans now live in counties with only one or no source of local news. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Those closures have been shown to have a significant effect on political division. In a study assessing the relationship between newspaper closures and polarized voting, Dunaway and colleagues found that split-ticket voting — when people vote for candidates of different parties on the same ballot — decreased by a small but notable 1.9 percent in communities that had lost a newspaper before the 2012 election. A factor driving polarization, she explains, is that Americans’ attention has shifted to the national stage. “Most of the political news stories are framed in terms of the parties waging wars against each other,” says Dunaway, “whereas local news is more about the issues that face your school district, your garbage collection, the potholes, traffic — things that are less partisan in nature.” Dunaway’s study of voting patterns caught the eye of Julie Makinen, then-executive editor of the Desert Sun newspaper in southern California. Makinen launched an experiment: For a month, the opinion section ditched syndicated columns and letters about national disputes for locally authored commentaries and California-focused political cartoons. Credit: City Bureau “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community.” —Julie Makinen The test provided a living lab for Dunaway and her colleagues. They found that removing national politics from the opinion section didn’t reverse polarization in the Palm Springs region, but it did slow down feelings of distance between people of different political positions. The exact cause of this is unclear, according to Dunaway. Is it from increasing attention on less ideologically divided local issues? Or reducing consumption of national, more partisan news? But one of the clearest insights, she says, is that it’s viable for publications to reduce national news coverage. “People had opinions and complaints, but they, on the whole, were mostly glad to see less national stuff and more local.” For Makinen, the experience speaks to the importance of forums for civil discussion about local issues. And the community seemed to agree. When Gannett, the paper’s owner, discontinued the opinion section, community members worked with Makinen to raise money to continue to pay for an opinion editor. That fundraising effort became the Coachella Valley Journalism Foundation , a nonprofit that now supports newsrooms across the region with trainings, awards and funding for newsroom jobs. The stories local outlets cover about what’s happening at the city and county level have a much bigger impact on people’s lives than the national stage, Makinen notes. And, they create openings where community members can build relationships with each other. “Local news gives people so many different touch points to connect with people in their community, and sort of feel less isolated and polarized,” she says. Documenters is one way local news is helping community members find those touch points. The approach to citizen journalism was developed in Chicago by the nonprofit news outlet City Bureau, when the editorial team decided to recruit residents to help comb through a massive police document. It would have taken one reporter dozens of hours alone, explains Resnik. But by bringing in residents interested in flexing their research muscles, the outlet expanded its capacity and built new relationships with the community. Participants at a Documenters training session. Credit: City Bureau That evolved into Documenters, a model Resnik describes as a “civic side hustle,” where community members are paid a stipend to, as he says, “commit these small acts of journalism.” The approach has since been adopted in 25 communities, each run locally by a news or civic organization. In Ohio, Signal Akron launched three years ago simultaneously with their Documenters program, building the network of residents into the way the publication operates. Each week, community editor Kevin Dilley recruits from a pool of more than 400 trained Documenters to cover about a dozen local meetings. Documenters apply to cover meetings as fits their schedule, and make about $90 per meeting. They write up summaries, highlighting a few points they find most important. After some light editing, summaries are posted on the Documenters Akron website. If something particularly noteworthy happens, the summary may get published on Signal Akron’s main website, alongside stories written by the outlet’s professional journalists. The program, according to Dilley, has resulted in an extraordinarily diverse newsroom. Documenters range in age from 19 to 84, some with PhDs, others reentering from incarceration. Every zip code in the greater Akron area is represented. For Dilley, this community-driven approach provides an opportunity to rebuild trust in local news. Residents may be skeptical of news media, and even of Signal Akron. “Here’s the thing with the Documenters,” he says. “You trust your neighbors.” One of the biggest challenges is funding. In Akron, there are more public meetings — and more Documenters interested in covering them — than the small editorial team can handle. Dunaway, of Syracuse University, notes that there is a resurgence of attention on local news. With the internet, many anticipated that online sources about hyperlocal news issues would naturally emerge, but it didn’t happen. Now, she notes, there are concerted efforts to boost local news coverage in order to fill the need. So far, however, she says they tend to be scattershot. Urban areas tend to be better served, while rural and lower-income communities are less well-covered. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime What exactly local news looks like is also changing. Across the country, Documenters share information through messaging networks, bulletin boards and conversations with neighbors. And instead of framing local elections in the national two-party horserace, Documenters have focused on making sure community members understand the roles of the municipal positions on the ballot. “It changes this idea of an ‘us v. them’ into something where there’s much, much more nuance,” Resnik says. Jantzi believes every community should have something like a Documenters program. It’s not that local politics aren’t divisive, she says. Police issues tend to be highly polarized, and school board meetings get so contentious they stretch for hours. But by seeing meetings play out, and connecting with neighbors who are interested, there’s more awareness of the nuances of local governance. “There’s just more accountability for the decision-making and more power to the community to actually learn what’s happening,” she says. The post Want the News to Unite People? Let Them Report It appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Burrowing Owls Nesting on Solar Farms are Rewriting a Species’ Future Reading Time: 3 minutes Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are showing that clean energy and wildlife habitat can share the same land. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms are turning a renewable energy site into an unlikely nursery. More than a dozen owlets hatched this summer inside plastic tunnels at a 10,000-acre solar complex near Phoenix, Arizona. The project suggests clean energy and vulnerable wildlife can thrive side by side. Longroad Energy, the solar company that runs the site, teamed up with Wild at Heart , a raptor rehabilitation center. Together they set out to test whether burrowing owls nesting on solar farms could raise families long-term. In March, workers moved nine owl pairs and one single male about 50 miles to the site, since their old burrows were about to be destroyed by new housing. Burrowing owls are small, ground-dwelling birds of prey roughly the size of a loaf of bread, perched on long, stilt-like legs. They typically nest in tunnels dug by animals like ground squirrels and prairie dogs. Since the 1960s, their numbers have dropped by more than a third across the United States. Housing and farmland development keep shrinking that habitat. Conservation groups often relocate colonies before bulldozers arrive, moving them to farmland where they can hunt. But as farmland gets bought up too, safe new sites are harder to find. The Wild at Heart’s Burrowing Owl team had nearly run out of nearby options. They used to drive displaced owls about 50 miles to open farmland. Now some trips stretch 60 to 100 miles, which is too costly to sustain, even though the owls need very little space to settle in. Solar farms offered a new possibility for relocation. Utility-scale solar energy, meaning large power plants built to serve the electric grid, has expanded quickly across Arizona. That growth can squeeze desert wildlife, but it also helps slow climate change, a threat already putting many U.S. bird species at risk. State law required Longroad to survey wildlife before building its Sun Streams project. That survey found eight burrowing owls already living on the land. The discovery connected the company with Wild at Heart, which was running low on relocation space, sparking a larger experiment in burrowing owls nesting on solar farms. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms emerged as a conservation solution when Longroad Energy’s pre-construction wildlife survey found eight owls already living on the land, connecting the company with Wild at Heart at a moment when the raptor center was running out of relocation space for displaced desert birds. Photo by Greg Clark courtesy of Wild at Heart . After construction finished, Longroad offered Wild at Heart around 250 acres between two Sun Streams projects. Workers installed 40 artificial burrows and placed a breeding pair in each, at first surrounded by netting so the birds would not fly back home. They also set up lights to attract insects and delivered mice daily while the owls adjusted. The company funded feeding and monitoring through the entire breeding season, support Wild at Heart normally cannot afford beyond 30 days. Within one month, every female had laid eggs, an early sign that burrowing owls nesting on solar farms might actually work. By late June, 36 chicks had hatched. Within three months, 29 young owls had fledged and left the nest, and staff slowly stopped feeding them so the birds would learn to hunt on their own. The team began spotting insect remains in their droppings, an encouraging sign. By the end of August, Wild at Heart stopped feedings altogether. Researchers are now studying how to expand this kind of coexistence. A 2025 Arizona State University study found that prime solar sites overlap with burrowing owl habitat by about 13% across seven Western states. The nonprofit Renewable Energy Wildlife Institute is building a database to help solar companies weigh biodiversity when choosing where to build. Arizona is also drafting guidelines to help future solar projects support wildlife instead of displacing it. Wild at Heart hopes to grow vegetation on solar sites to attract insects and rodents for owls to eat, turning relocation sites into lasting habitat. Longroad is even discussing solar panel designs that could capture water from humid air to help plants grow nearby. Small changes like that could make future sites more welcoming for burrowing owls nesting on solar farms from day one. The raptor conservation group hopes to bring more solar companies on board. Burrowing owls nesting on solar farms may soon become less of an experiment and more of a model other developers can copy. If more companies adopt the practice, displaced owl colonies could find lasting homes on the very land built to power their neighbors. For a bird that has lost so much ground, that shift offers a real reason for hope. The post How Burrowing Owls Nesting on Solar Farms are Rewriting a Species’ Future appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Comoros Turns Climate Ambition into Action with a Plan Focused on Forests, Water, and Geothermal Energy Reading Time: 3 minutes Despite producing almost no greenhouse gas emissions, the Comoros is turning climate ambition into action through a $6.6 billion national plan backed by forest restoration, water security projects, and a new geothermal power plant. Turning climate ambition into action is now central to how the Union of Comoros plans its future . This volcanic archipelago on the Southeastern African side of the Indian Ocean produces almost no greenhouse gas emissions of its own. Yet it faces some of the world’s most severe climate risks. The country is also a global biodiversity hotspot, home to unique forests and coral reefs. Roughly a fifth of the population already lives in poverty, with another fifth at risk. Cyclones and droughts threaten to push even more families into hardship each year. In the last decade, two major cyclones have struck the islands hard. Cyclone Kenneth affected 40% of the population in 2019. Cyclone Chido followed in 2024, again damaging homes, crops, and infrastructure. In March 2026, the Comoros submitted an updated climate plan to the United Nations. The plan, called a Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC, sets ambitious new targets. It aims to cut emissions by 14 to 57 percent by 2035, depending on outside support. Full implementation of the plan is expected to cost about $6.6 billion by 2030. The UN Development Programme (UNDP), is helping the country secure that funding. Early support has already unlocked millions of dollars from international climate funds. Adaptation sits at the heart of the country’s climate strategy. The Comoros plans to reforest 8,000 hectares of land over the coming years. It also aims to restore 1,000 hectares of mangroves and 600 hectares of coral reefs. Agriculture depends heavily on a healthy environment across the islands. Export crops like vanilla, ylang-ylang, and cloves support many rural livelihoods. Protecting these value chains from climate shocks is now a funding priority for UNDP and its partners. Forest and mangrove restoration could bring added financial benefits over time. The Comoros is exploring carbon credit markets under the Paris Agreement’s Article 6. Its forestry and mangrove sectors may become key assets for future carbon projects. Water security remains an urgent challenge across the islands. Grande Comore has no permanent rivers and relies mainly on rainfall. The government plans to build 50 micro-dams and restore 6,000 hectares of watersheds. UNDP has already helped install climate-resilient water infrastructure in more than 50 communities. This work now serves more than 230,000 people across the islands. Local residents help maintain the boreholes, treatment plants, and reservoirs themselves. Turning climate ambition into action in the Comoros means building on UNDP’s climate-resilient water infrastructure already serving more than 230,000 people across the islands through community-maintained boreholes, treatment plants, and reservoirs. Photo courtesy of UNDP . Energy remains one of the country’s biggest sources of emissions. Diesel generators currently supply much of the electricity used in Comorian homes. Turning climate ambition into action here means building a cleaner power grid. A geothermal power plant near the Karthala volcano could help change that. Geoscience surveys have confirmed strong potential for high-temperature energy there. The project is now moving through exploration and risk-reduction studies. Planners expect the plant to generate around 15 megawatts once complete. Funding partners include the African Development Bank and the Global Environment Facility. Italy is also funding technical support to help make the project attractive to future investors. Smaller renewable projects are also expanding access to clean power. UNDP is testing solar minigrids on three separate islands. Each design includes ways for women and young people to take part. Disaster preparedness is another growing focus for the country. New data tools helped teams respond faster after Cyclone Chido struck in 2024. The government is also developing new insurance products for vulnerable communities. A national disaster risk reduction strategy now guides these efforts through 2030. The plan has already helped attract financing from the World Bank and the African Development Bank. Turning climate ambition into action increasingly means matching local plans with international partners. The full strategy appears in the country’s official Nationally Determined Contribution, filed with the United Nations. The plan also includes a social inclusion focus on women, youth, and vulnerable groups for the first time. Electricity access in the Comoros has grown from 46% in 2017 to 71% today. Each new project adds another piece to the country’s climate plan. Turning climate ambition into action, piece by piece, may be this island nation’s clearest path forward. items.descriptionOriginal: What happens when young people see a problem that others have learned to overlook? Across the United States, a growing network of students is rescuing millions of dollars' worth of perfectly usable medical supplies destined for landfills and delivering them to communities in need. When 16-year-old Ben Kurian discovered that hospitals routinely discarded sterile supplies simply because they were nearing expiration, he began organizing donations from his kitchen table. His efforts have since grown into a movement alongside student-led organizations like Blueprints for Pangea and United2Heal, whose volunteers are redirecting medical supplies to underserved clinics around the world. Balancing schoolwork with warehouse shifts and deliveries, these young changemakers are proving that compassion, resourcefulness, and a willingness to act can make an extraordinary difference. They didn't wait for someone else to solve the problem. They simply saw a need and got to work.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work. NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks. Teddy and everyone like him Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said. The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious. What happened after SNAP cuts St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget , pets included. “The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.” Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening. Where to find free pet food in NYC Here are all 22 participating locations: Bronx – Part of the Solution: 2759 Webster Ave., 10458 – New York Common Pantry: 1290 Hoe Ave., 10459 – Davidson Community Center: 2038 Davidson Ave., 10453 – The Kingsbridge Heights Community Center: 3067 Kingsbridge Terrace, 10463 Queens – First United Methodist Church of Jamaica: 162-10 Highland Ave., 11432 – River Fund: 89-11 Lefferts Boulevard, 11418 – Yeshua Worldwide Ministries Food Pantry: 7911 Caldwell Ave., 11379 – Hour Children Community Outreach: 36-49 11th Street, 11106 Brooklyn – Community Help in Park Slope: 200 Fourth Ave., 11217 – Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty: 5361 Preston Court, 11234 – On the Go Relief: 2832 Fulton Street, 11207 – St. John’s Bread and Life Food Pantry: 795 Lexington Ave., 11221 – The Campaign Against Hunger: 2004 Fulton Street, 11233 – YMCA Community Market: 2980 West 29th Street, 11224 Manhattan – Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen Pantry: 296 Ninth Ave., 10001 – New York Common Pantry: 8 East 109th Street, 10029 – St. Clemens Food Pantry: 423 West 46th Street, 10036 – The Father’s Heart Ministries: 543-545 East 11th Street, 10009 – The Lower Eastside Girls Club: 402 East 8th Street, 10009 – Trinity’s Services and Food for the Homeless: 602 East 9th Street, 10009 Staten Island – Project Hospitality: 205 Canal Street, 10304 – Feeding with TLC: 309 St. Paul’s Ave., 10304 Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Halloween might be the one night a year when the whole family ends up outside together, moving through the neighborhood in the dark. Whether that ends in magic or meltdown depends almost entirely on whether the experience matches the kid you brought with you. Dr. Kristen Cook , a board-certified pediatrician with more than 15 years of practice in the Midwest, writes that across every age, Halloween offers genuine opportunities to practice life skills like facing fears, managing expectations, developing independence, and showing kindness. How much kids are able to glean out spooky season depends on how you set it up. Toddlers and preschoolers: small excursion, low stimulation The tricky thing about Halloween for little kids is that everything exciting about it is also a lot. Unfamiliar noises, scary decorations , a neighborhood full of costumed kids running in every direction; it can tip from exciting to overwhelming fast. Dr. Cook’s rule for this age: comfortable over elaborate. Costumes shouldn’t restrict movement or vision, and there’s no reason to push through the full neighborhood circuit after dark. An early start, before it gets busy, tends to go better. Bring a wagon or stroller even if your toddler insists they don’t need one because, let’s face it, they probably will. Inspect every piece of candy before it’s touched, check for choking hazards and allergens, and agree on a daily candy limit in advance so it’s not a negotiation every time. And if the evening tips into over-stimulation, head home. A short, good Halloween beats a long, tearful one. School-age kids: independence with eyes on Elementary-age kids are ready for more. They can choose their own costumes, help decorate the house, pick out pumpkins , and have real opinions about the trick-or-treating route. Dr. Cook recommends mapping that route together in advance and letting kids take the lead once you’re out. That said, supervision doesn’t disappear. Pumpkin carving is still an adult activity at this age, and a parent or trusted adult should remain part of the outing, even if they’re hanging back a house or two. Night-friendly costume details matter more here. Think glow bracelets, LED accessories, and reflective elements. The shift at this stage is toward earned independence. Let them decide who they trick-or-treat with. Let them handle their own candy negotiations. Keep the safety guardrails in place, but make room for them to feel the difference. Teenagers: expectations and exit plans By the teenage years, Halloween looks different. Some teens feel too old for trick-or-treating; others still want to be part of it. Dr. Cook’s take is not to push them out of it. Teenagers who help hand out candy, look after younger siblings, or supervise part of the evening have a real role that doesn’t require a costume. If they’re going out independently, the conversations to have are about curfew, approved locations, and what to do if they end up somewhere uncomfortable. Dr. Cook specifically recommends creating an exit plan before they leave, so they have a way out of an uncomfortable situation without needing to explain themselves in the moment. A standing offer of a no-questions pickup goes a long way. The bigger ask for teenagers is respect. Taking more than a reasonable amount from an unattended candy bowl, or pulling pranks that leave families upset, isn’t harmless fun. Dr. Cook frames this as a chance to practice the kind of independence that looks like actual maturity. What all ages have in common The memories that stick, Dr. Cook writes, usually aren’t about the costumes or the candy. They’re about the feelings that are attached to them. They remember feeling included, connected, part of something. Halloween doesn’t require expensive gear or elaborate setups. It requires showing up for the kid in front of you, at whatever stage they’re at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: The Sydney Opera House, with its bold, innovative architecture, is said to be one of the world’s most photographed buildings — and it may soon share that status with another venue of its kind. Opening last week along China’s Huangpu River, the Shanghai Grand Opera House truly lives up to the adjective in its title. At nearly 1.6 million square feet, the performing arts center has three auditoriums seating 4,200 guests in total and will showcase everything from baroque opera and classical music to experimental productions. But what is perhaps its most awe-worthy attraction lies not within its walls but outside them: a stunning, spiral staircase that appears to be almost suspended in air. Yumeng Zhu The staircase connects the ground level to a rooftop observation deck that also serves as a stage, and visitors can access it regardless of whether they’re attending a show (cue the onslaught of social media selfies). Yumeng Zhu Restaurants, galleries, educational facilities, and other public spaces in and around the building are designed to welcome residents and tourists alike, positioning the opera house as a cultural landmark more than merely a ticketed institution. View this post on Instagram “People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” Kjetil Thorsen, co-founder of Norway-based firm Snøhetta, which designed the building, told Dezeen. “A successful landmark is not only recognized by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.” Snøhetta’s proposal won an international competition in 2016, and the firm teamed up with East China Architectural Design & Research Institute, Theatre Projects, and Nagata Acoustics in 2019 to bring the project from concept to completion. Wang Xiang—Xinhua/Getty Images The 2,000-seat main auditorium, called Harmony Hall, has five levels and three balconies. Soar Theatre, with a capacity of 1,200, is intended for more intimate productions, like operettas and plays, while the third auditorium, dubbed Open Stage, seats 1,000 and features adaptable stage and seating configurations, making it ideal for experimental works. The theme of movement was intentionally woven into the building’s architecture and aesthetic, a nod to the flowing river it sits adjacent to and the bustling city in which it’s located. Large glass windows let ample light in during the day and shift the mood for visitors as the sun sets or the weather changes. Tall outdoor towers are illuminated at night, marking the venue’s place within Shanghai’s skyline. Yumeng Zhu “A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of,” Thorsen told Dezeen. “When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context.” RELATED: “First of Its Kind”: World’s Longest Outdoor Escalator Opens in China — Take a Virtual Ride

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Testing SEHMUA Infrared Solar Wildlife and Security Cameras Reading Time: 3 minutes The SEHMUA infrared solar wildlife and security camera pairs clean solar charging with invisible night vision to observe wildlife without disruption. The home security company SEHMUA recently sent Happy Eco News a two-pack of its 2K Solar Security Cameras Wireless Outdoor for review. My recent move to a rural property provided the ideal setting to test this sponsored package. SEHMUA offered me these cameras as a home security measure, but I live in a really safe area. Property crime is not really an issue here. I said yes because rather than record human intruders, my goal is to observe local wildlife cleanly, without running invasive power cords across the land. Living alongside nature means sharing boundary land with raccoons, black-tailed deer, and, a couple of times a month, mountain lions (cougars), as neighbors report. Using an infrared solar wildlife and security camera offers an easy way to secure my property while observing wildlife and other animals that may visit when I am not home. The SEHMUA IR night vision security cameras work for wildlife too. Licensed under the Unsplash+ License Each unit pairs with a detachable solar panel and an internal rechargeable battery. Sunlight powers the hardware continuously through daylight hours. As a result, users never need to haul heavy extension cords outside or take the gear down to recharge. Hardware setup takes about five minutes per unit on an exterior wall, tree post, or fence line. The wire-free design eliminates the need to drill through exterior frames or hire an electrician. The camera delivers 2K high-definition video. A 2K image contains double the clarity of standard 1080p high definition. This sharp resolution lets property owners verify distinct coat markings, antler points, or paw prints across the perimeter. A motorized lens rotates 355 degrees horizontally and tilts 90 degrees vertically to create a 360-degree panoramic view. One device can follow a foraging raccoon across a fence line that normally requires several fixed lenses. Each unit relies on a Passive Infrared sensor, known as a PIR sensor. A PIR sensor detects living body heat rather than blowing grass or swaying tree limbs. This heat-detection focus cuts out nuisance phone alerts while ensuring deer or cougars trigger instant recordings. The unit includes 500-lumen white spotlights and an intruder alarm for standard security deterrence. Obviously, when monitoring wildlife, sudden white light can startle shy animals and disrupt natural foraging habits. Switching the unit to infrared camera mode avoids this issue. Black-and-white infrared night vision uses invisible light beams to film nighttime visitors clearly up to 98 feet away without frightening them. This passive approach supports ethical wildlife observation. Homeowners can observe natural behaviors without feeding animals, baiting them, or disrupting their regular travel routes. Precise video timestamps also help map local wildlife activity patterns. Logging the exact arrival times of visiting deer, mountain lions, or raccoons reveals recurring habits. Knowing these schedules allows us to bring pets indoors well before large predators begin their evening hunt. Two-way audio allows owners to listen to ambient forest sounds directly through a smartphone. If an unwelcome predator (animal or human) approaches, I can manually trigger a 110-decibel siren. The hardware connects over standard 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi networks. It does not connect over 5 gigahertz bands. The manufacturer notes the camera operates reliably between minus 4 degrees and 122 degrees Fahrenheit. An IP65 weather rating protects the electronics against driving rain, snow, and wind. Footage saves directly to a local Micro SD card holding up to 128 gigabytes. This local storage setup avoids monthly cloud fees while saving hours of midnight animal visits. An optional cloud trial is also available for 30 days. Deploying an infrared solar wildlife and security camera gives rural residents peace of mind. Homeowners gain a non-invasive window into natural wildlife habits while safeguarding their homestead with clean solar energy. So far, I am impressed and will be doing a video review on the Happy Eco News YouTube channel in the coming weeks. The cameras are available through Amazon or directly from SEHMUA online. The post Testing SEHMUA Infrared Solar Wildlife and Security Cameras appeared first on Happy Eco News .
