items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester Reading Time: 3 minutes A farming byproduct that has filled pillows in Japan for generations is giving sleepers a plastic-free way to rest, and it can go back to the soil when it wears out. Every night, most of us rest our heads on a bag of plastic. Polyester fiber and memory foam, the two most common pillow fillings, are both made from fossil fuels. They clump, collect sweat and dust, and go flat within a year or two. Then the pillow gets thrown out. Most curbside recycling programs won’t take it, so it ends up in a landfill or an incinerator, and the cycle starts again with a new one. A growing number of sleepers are breaking that cycle with a leftover from buckwheat farming. A buckwheat pillow is filled with the hard outer shells of buckwheat seeds, the part nobody eats. Buckwheat is grown for its seeds, which are turned into flour, groats and noodles. Before the seed can be eaten, its tough, triangular shell has to be removed. Those shells, called hulls, are a byproduct of the milling process. Some are used for animal bedding or burned for fuel, but many have little value. Using hulls as pillow filling turns that waste stream into a useful product, in the same spirit as researchers turning leftover straw into crop waste fabric for clothing. No extra land is needed, because the hulls come from a crop that is already being grown for food. Pillows filled with buckwheat hulls have been used in Japan for generations, where they are known as sobakawa pillows. Their growing popularity in Europe and North America has more to do with materials: many shoppers now want a pillow that isn’t made from plastic. The crop itself also has a relatively light footprint. Buckwheat grows quickly, tolerates poor soils and generally needs little fertilizer. Its white flowers attract bees and other pollinators, and farmers often plant it as a cover crop to suppress weeds and protect the soil between other plantings. That doesn’t make every buckwheat pillow automatically green. Where the hulls are grown, how far they travel and how they are processed all make a difference. Hulls that are grown, milled and made into pillows in the same region carry far fewer transport emissions than those shipped across continents. No Fluff Pillow is one example of how short that supply chain can be. Its hulls come from a local buckwheat farm and are mechanically cleaned multiple times to remove dust and small particles. Each pillow is then filled by hand with 3.4 kg of hulls. Comfort is a big part of the appeal. Foam and polyester tend to trap heat, while hulls leave small air gaps between them so air keeps circulating. Many sleepers find that a buckwheat pillow stays noticeably cooler through the night. Buckwheat pillows also last much longer than conventional ones. Polyester fibers clump and foam gradually loses its shape, and neither can be repaired. Once they break down, the whole pillow has to be thrown away. Buckwheat hulls are hard and hold their shape for years. They slowly compress with use, and some break into smaller pieces, but owners can top the pillow up with fresh hulls or replace the filling entirely while keeping the same cover. Most buckwheat pillows also have a zipper, so sleepers can add or remove hulls to adjust height and firmness. One pillow can suit back, side and stomach sleepers, and a change in sleeping position doesn’t require a new purchase. When a buckwheat pillow finally does reach the end of its life, very little of it has to be thrown away. The hulls are plant material and can be added to a home compost pile or a yard waste bin, where they break down and return nutrients to the soil. Gardeners also use them as mulch. The cotton cover can be washed and reused, cut into cleaning cloths or taken to a textile collection point. A foam pillow, by contrast, has no practical recycling route in most places and can take decades to break down. Lawmakers are starting to take notice. California’s SB 707, the first statewide textile recycling law in the US, now covers pillows and bedding, and every EU country must set up similar producer-funded schemes for textiles by 2028. Buckwheat pillows do come with trade-offs. They are much heavier than fiber pillows, often weighing several kilograms. They are firm, molding to the head and neck rather than squashing flat, and most people need a few nights to adjust. They also rustle softly whenever the sleeper moves, a sound most people stop noticing within a week. Shoppers considering the switch can check where the hulls were grown and milled, how thoroughly they were cleaned, whether the cover is made from natural fibers such as organic cotton, and whether the pillow can be refilled rather than replaced. For households already composting food scraps or cutting back on plastic, the pillow is one of the easier swaps to make. The post Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home Reading Time: 4 minutes Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home Key Takeaways Plan around daily frustrations before choosing colors, tile, or fixtures. Prioritize safe shower access, reliable lighting, clear pathways, and moisture control. Select durable surfaces, simple fixtures, and storage that reduce routine cleaning and clutter. Consider household needs today while preparing for future changes in mobility needs. Build a budget that includes waterproofing, labor, permits, ventilation, and potential hidden repairs. A bathroom should support the way people actually live, from rushed weekday mornings to relaxed evening showers. A well-planned bathroom remodel can solve practical problems such as a high tub wall, poor lighting, cluttered counters, slippery flooring, or surfaces that require constant scrubbing. The best results come from treating the room as a connected system. Layout, drainage, ventilation, lighting, storage, and finishes all affect comfort, cleaning, and long-term performance. Start with the issues that make daily routines harder, then choose design details that support the solutions. Why Practical Planning Matters A remodel that looks appealing but ignores everyday inconveniences can become frustrating quickly. For example, a homeowner may love a decorative tile sample but discover that the new shower still has a difficult entry, no place to store toiletries, and dim lighting near the mirror. Addressing the function first makes it easier to select finishes that work with the room rather than against it. Inspect the Existing Bathroom Before demolition or shopping for products, inspect the room closely. Look for cracked tile, loose flooring, damaged caulk, water stains, soft walls, slow drains, peeling paint, and recurring mildew. Notice where water lands after a shower and whether the door, drawers, and cabinets open without blocking the walkway. Test switches, outlets, plumbing fixtures, and the exhaust fan. A fan that makes noise is not necessarily moving air outside effectively. Signs of plumbing leaks, electrical issues, extensive moisture damage, or a weakened subfloor should be evaluated by a qualified professional before selecting finishes. Set Clear Remodeling Priorities Separate your wish list into three categories so essential work remains protected if costs change: Must-haves: Repairs, waterproofing, safe entry, dependable lighting, and ventilation. Useful upgrades: Better storage, a handheld showerhead, seating, improved mirrors, and accessible controls. Optional details: Accent walls, premium hardware, decorative lighting, and smart features. Choose a Safer Shower Layout A standard bathtub, a tub-and-shower combination, a walk-in shower, a low-threshold shower, and a curbless shower can all be appropriate choices. The right option depends on the room’s size, plumbing arrangement, whether children use the bathroom, and the household’s current and future needs. For a shower-focused remodel, useful features can include accessible controls, a handheld showerhead, recessed niches, secure grab bars, and space to move near the entry. The home safety steps for preventing falls include brighter lighting, clear walking areas, and grab bars around tubs, showers, and toilets. Curbless showers can improve access, but they require careful attention to floor slope, drainage, waterproofing, and code-compliant installation. Improve Flooring and Lighting Bathroom flooring should be made for wet conditions and have a surface texture suited to areas that may become damp. Highly polished finishes can be harder to navigate when wet. Keep the route from the shower to towels and storage as short and uncluttered as possible, and use bath mats with stable, slip-resistant backing. Layered lighting makes routines easier. General ceiling lighting brightens the room; vanity lighting helps with grooming; shower lighting improves visibility in the bathing area; and low-level night lighting can make late-night trips more comfortable. Place switches where they are easy to reach when entering the room. Select Easier-to-Clean Materials Materials affect how much time a bathroom requires each week. Large-format tile can mean fewer grout lines than a small mosaic pattern, while smooth wall panels and nonporous counters can simplify wiping down wet areas. Simple faucet forms with fewer tight crevices are often easier to clean than highly detailed designs. Low-maintenance does not mean maintenance-free. Any shower wall, countertop, fixture, or floor still needs routine cleaning, sound installation, and prompt attention to damaged caulk or grout. Plan Storage Around Daily Routines Storage works best when it matches the items used every day. Keep frequently used toiletries between knee and shoulder height, use vanity drawers or pull-outs for small items, and place towels close to the shower or bath. Recessed niches can provide convenient shower storage when wall conditions allow. Medicines should be kept away from humid bathroom conditions, and reducing floor clutter can also reduce unnecessary bending and reaching. Control Moisture and Improve Ventilation Moisture can damage finishes and contribute to repeated mildew, condensation, musty odors, and peeling paint. An exhaust fan should vent outdoors rather than into an attic or another enclosed area. The EPA explains that bathroom ventilation removes unwanted moisture and recommends checking that the fan is functioning properly during renovation. Run the fan during bathing and afterward to help clear humid air. Also, inspect caulked joints, shower doors, and plumbing connections regularly, since small leaks are easier to address before they damage walls or flooring. Add Helpful Universal Design Features Universal design can look polished and inviting rather than clinical. Lever handles, handheld showerheads, comfortable fixture heights, wider clearances, seating, and contrast between controls and surrounding surfaces can support a wider range of users. If future grab bars may be helpful, plan wall reinforcement before the walls are closed. This small decision can make later updates simpler. Build a Realistic Budget and Remodeling Plan A complete budget should account for design, demolition, disposal, plumbing, electrical work, waterproofing, ventilation, flooring, wall finishes, lighting, fixtures, storage, permits, inspections, labor, and cleanup. Set aside a contingency amount for concealed leaks, damaged subfloors, or outdated plumbing that may be discovered after demolition. Compare detailed proposals rather than choosing only the lowest total. Then follow a clear sequence: List daily problems and measure the room. Choose must-haves before optional upgrades. Select the tub or shower layout. Coordinate lighting, ventilation, storage, and safety features. Review estimates, permits, scheduling, cleanup, and warranties. Test drainage, doors, drawers, lights, and fixtures during the final walkthrough. Common Bathroom Remodeling Questions Does a safer bathroom have to look clinical? No. Coordinated hardware, warm finishes, modern lighting, and built-in storage can make safety-minded features feel like a natural part of the design. Is a walk-in shower always better than a bathtub? No. A walk-in shower may improve access and reduce cleaning around a tub wall, while a bathtub can remain useful for children or household members who enjoy soaking. What should be checked at the final walkthrough? Confirm shower drainage and water flow, fixture stability, door and drawer clearance, switch placement, accessible storage, caulk details, cleanup quality, and warranty documents. Final Planning Tips Start with safety, moisture control, lighting, storage, and durable surfaces. Choose lasting features for the room’s permanent parts, then add personality with paint, mirrors, hardware, and accessories that are easier to change. A thoughtful plan can create a bathroom that looks finished, functions comfortably, and continues to support the household for years. The post Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Permaculture farmer Chau Quang Duong explains how the microbes that support life make up only 5% of the organic matter in living soil. Using artificial means, such as chemicals, for speed and efficiency can readily destroy those microbes making the soil dry, hard, and lifeless. In the same way, Chau cautions, when we give up our inner wisdom in total reliance on AI in the interest of speed, efficiency, and “perfection,” we risk destroying the living culture and knowledge of a local place from which life and our own inner wisdom grows – the 5% that AI can never provide. He suggests the need to continually replenish the soil of the soul through deep connection, such as immersion in a garden. “Just as the soil can recover when we stop damaging it and begin to care for it, our inner lives can become fertile again when we give ourselves time, space, and a deeper connection with nature.” “When the mind releases its need to control everything, a quiet, open space appears. In that space, our inner voice can begin to speak again.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Saul Levmore and Ward Farnsworth are college professors, so it’s fitting that the title of their new book is a question rather than an answer (beyond it being a fair way to pique interest). Like all good teachers, the authors don’t just want us to learn — they want us to learn how to think . In Should You Tip for Takeout? , they mine the fields of law, economics, philosophy, sports, and rhetoric to present a “tool kit for a more rational life.” Far from being an etiquette guide, it’s instead an invitation to expand the way we look at the world, so we can better understand not only our own behavior but others’ as well. Each chapter uses a common quandary — like whether you should recline your airplane seat or get a second opinion before surgery — as a jumping-off point to introduce heuristics and critical thinking techniques that can be applied to countless other scenarios. The resulting pages offer up food for thought and fodder for lighthearted debates. “One way to think about it is we’re trying to write a book that helps people have more fun having conversations at the dinner table,” Farnsworth explained in an interview with Nice News, noting that discussions these days seem to so easily devolve into political arguments or fear-based speculations about the future. “We thought, ‘You know, there’s a lot of things just in everyday life that are actually pretty interesting to think about if you look more closely at them than most people usually do,’” he said, adding: “What would it mean to really take this one apart rationally? What can you learn about the problem that makes everyday life a little more interesting, and maybe what can you learn about rationality that makes other things easier to understand?” Again, anyone hoping for simple “yes” or “no” solutions to life’s dilemmas would be opening the wrong book. In a chapter called “Should You Keep Looking for a Better Price?,” for example, the authors encourage readers to acquaint themselves with distribution patterns and standard deviations. In another, they demonstrate how one might use the mathematical theory of optimal stopping to choose a romantic partner. (Essentially: View the first 37% of your dates or relationships as a comparison pool, and then pick the first subsequent person who’s better than the best one in the sample cohort.) Photo by Lloyd DeGrane from UChicago Saul Levmore That’s not to say there are no straightforward answers. The title chapter delves into the power we have with our wallets to vote for or against a custom when it hasn’t yet become a norm. If something has become entrenched, it’s likely in our best interest to go along with it, whether or not we agree. In the case of tipping for takeout, the authors say that the verdict is in: It’s the norm, so you should tip what you deem a reasonable amount. And doing so may not matter as much to your pocket as you might imagine. “Think of it as a hidden price hike,” Farnsworth said. “But the good news is that you have something to say about it. You have some discretion on how much you’re going to let that price go up. And that should be considered a welcome thing rather than a bad thing, because the alternative is the price goes up for everybody.” The authors said that simply musing through these kinds of common scenarios can reveal possibilities one may never have considered for why things are the way they are and what alternatives exist. Courtesy of Godine Ward Farnsworth “One broad takeaway to me is that people should experiment more in their own lives,” Levmore said, adding, “I think the book tries to encourage people to imagine how the world could be a little bit different from the way it is.” It may also help expand our empathy, Farnsworth pointed out. “Sometimes looking at life and looking for the rationality in it is a way to be more generous-minded toward other people who appear to just be annoying you at random and may be doing just what you would do if you were in their shoes.” When our conversation turned to the most favorable order in which to be interviewed for a job, the pair demonstrated — perhaps unintentionally — just how the aforementioned dinner table discourse may go. “I think it’s a disadvantage to be the last person,” Levmore said, prompting Farnsworth to disagree: “I generally think you want to go last. You want to go as late as you can.” “They get tired,” Levmore rejoined after Farnsworth elaborated, to which Farnsworth replied, “Maybe,” then added: “There’s no right answer to these questions. We just think these problems that most of us sort of wander through unconsciously, they’re just more interesting when you slow down and really ask, ‘What is the best way to handle this?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: A 50-year-old Japanese planting method is quietly reshaping vacant lots, schoolyards, and parking strips across the United States -- not through large-scale industrial effort, but through the hands of neighbors who show up on a Saturday to tuck seedlings into carefully prepared soil. Developed by botanist Akira Miyawaki, the method skips the slow prologue of natural forest succession, mixing climax species and their supporting plants to create self-sustaining ecosystems within decades rather than centuries. What makes it remarkable is not just the science but the ritual embedded in it: "He would take each plant, and the community had to say its name," recalls one organizer -- "it was about restoring relationships between humans and non-humans." The miniforest movement asks something modest of each participant and returns something harder to name: a sense of belonging to a place, and a stake in its future.

Οι θερμοκοιτίδες μπορεί επίσης να είναι κρίσιμες για τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Skin-to-skin contact, the practice of a newborn being placed directly onto the mother’s or father’s chest, is considered essential — sometimes lifesaving — care for preterm infants. The World Health Organization recommends it for at least eight hours a day beginning at birth for all babies born before 37 weeks. Incubators can also be critical for these newborns, however, and yet the carefully controlled environments prevent parents from performing that crucial skin-to-skin contact. A pioneering new technology has now bridged the two forms of care, allowing parents to hold their babies to their bodies without disrupting the essential treatments they require. Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital The Skincubator is a wearable medical tool designed for preterm infants weighing under 4.4 pounds that enables prolonged skin-to-skin contact beginning as early as the day of birth. A couple at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston, Texas, recently became the first in the U.S. to experience the difference it can make. For about 10 days after their twins were born in August, Tiffany Ikwuagwu and Dorian Ojemen weren’t able to hold the babies, who arrived at just 26 weeks. “This is a great invention,” Ikwuagwu, herself an obstetrician and gynecologist, said in a video from Memorial Hermann upon using the Skincubator. “I think the fact that I can help regulate the babies’ heart[s] and help the babies relax and just have that connection to them, is very special.” Added Ojemen in an interview with CNN earlier this month: “Just the fact that you can have them on your chest, you can look in their eyes, you can hold them, feel them breathe, like, that immediately makes you feel like, wow, I’m a parent.” The tech, which was developed over four years, was granted FDA Breakthrough Device designation last December. With the Skincubator, parents can relax or rest while bonding with their baby for hours at a time, taking turns with other caregivers and family members if they so choose. Infants’ arterial, umbilical, feeding, and airway tubes all remain in place. “The baby is already in their incubator, and they’re transferred from the incubator to the Skincubator while they’re in their isolate,” explained Dr. Jaclyn Ruggiero, principal investigator for an ongoing clinical trial, adding: “The baby’s medical lines and breathing tubes or breathing support are all secured to the Skincubator base. And the way the baby gets into skin-to-skin care is there’s a retractable pad under the baby, and that pad is pulled down slowly.” Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital Skin-to-skin contact is standard practice for all babies, helping to stabilize their heart rate and breathing, stimulating digestion, regulating temperature, providing protection against infection, and fostering the bond between parent and child. “It turns on a part of the nervous system that’s really important for connection and feeling calm,” Ruggiero said. Per the website, clinicians interested in bringing Skincubators to their NICUs can book a call with the company to begin a pilot program. Learn more.
